This economic test is deliberately not a mission-permission test. A row is deployable only if (1) its docking, modularity, refueling, depot, recycling, cooperative-target, and relocation requirements are technically satisfied; (2) Eq. (26) is nonnegative; and (3) every applicable authorization record is validated. The decision surface resolves 400-km and 650-km LEO, GEO, cislunar staging, LLO, and NRHO separately, including rendezvous, inclination/routing, station-keeping, residence, atmospheric clearance, radiation, debris exposure, tracking, and disposal. It crosses two client classes—a prepared high-value spacecraft and a cheap, short-lived unprepared constellation unit—with a demonstrator, regional servicer/depot fleet, and circular network. The last two amortize fixed cost over more clients but pay explicit scheduling, replenishment, routing, and congestion multipliers.

Download original CSV (232 KB) records all 324 combinations; Download original CSV (2 KB) prevents Earth-orbit and lunar-orbit parameters from being silently shared; and Download original CSV (3 KB) exposes capacity and fixed cost per client. Technical feasibility and economic viability are reported even when governance is not ready. In the declared 400-km LEO/regional-fleet case, upgrade, refuel/life extension, and repair of the prepared high-value asset have positive modeled net value, whereas the unprepared short-life unit is technically eligible only for replacement or disposal and neither is economically positive. Moving from the single demonstrator to the circular network lowers the assumption-class fixed cost per 400-km LEO client from $26.90M to $3.77M while increasing annual modeled service capacity from 1.12 to 26.53 clients; congestion and scheduling penalties remain charged. These figures are scenario comparisons, not prices or forecasts.

The machine-readable governance register separately covers ownership and consent, operating authorization, liability allocation, export-control review, spectrum/orbit authorization, custody and provenance, and safety-critical recycled-material qualification. Treaty jurisdiction, ownership, authorization, and liability provide the boundary [S69]; current U.S. export rules expressly make some spacecraft servicing/control transfers review-dependent [S70]; and current FCC rules tie operations and end of life to authorized debris plans [S71]. Applicability remains jurisdiction- and mission-specific, so every non-validated item blocks a deployable claim rather than being converted into a probability or cost.

Collision-cascade control boundary. Kessler risk is not an unusually large independent shock. It is positive feedback: collisions create orbiting fragments, those fragments raise the later collision rate, and a sufficiently dense region can keep generating debris after new deployment stops [S45]. The implemented LEO debris_event instead has a fixed 0.05 yr⁻¹ Poisson rate and removes a sampled 0.02–0.10 fraction from selected sectors; the loss creates no debris and the event rate does not depend on deployed capacity. The continuous catastrophic term is likewise an exogenous hazard range. These terms can represent ordinary impact exposure but cannot test the cascade threshold, avoidance saturation, shell-to-shell fragment transport, or recovery through decay and active removal. Accordingly, every LEO scale result in I.8 is conditional on a debris regime in which fragment creation does not outrun clearance. The missing state is not assigned a silent proxy value. The integrated layer supplies both an aggregate stress test and a second, finite-mass diagnostic resolving 400-km LEO, 650-km LEO, and cislunar regions; active assets, intact derelicts, trackable and untrackable fragments; collision-generated yield; avoidance saturation; cross-shell transport; disposal, natural clearance, retrieval, and active removal. It reports expected hazardous descendants per object as a branching-style stress metric (I.8, D.1). The kernels and transitions remain assumptions rather than a conjunction-assessment or validated traffic model. Lunar orbit does not remove the issue: breakup simulations find strongly orbit-dependent evolution, including long-lasting debris in some low lunar orbits and nonuniform lunar impact patterns [S46].

A deployable strategy begins with physical failure domains rather than a preferred logical cluster size. Let ℋt\mathcal H_t be the set of credible single-event exposure sets over a declared time window: collision pairs, breakup clouds, avoidance-coordination failures, and losses of shared power, gateway, navigation, software, or command services. The common-cause budget is

Lmax(t)=maxh∈ℋt∑iKi(t)𝟏[i∈h]≤ϵKtotal(t). L_{\max}(t) =\max_{h\in\mathcal H_t} \sum_i K_i(t)\,\mathbf 1[i\in h] \le \epsilon\,K_{\mathrm{total}}(t).

Each hazard set records altitude, inclination, plane, along-track extent, fragment correlation, shared services, and restoration window. Equation (27) makes allowable cluster size and reserve capacity outputs of geometry and risk tolerance. Capacity is distributed across independent domains so a damaged domain can be isolated, workloads rerouted, command and verification preserved, and reconstruction begun. Concentration gains—short links, shared power and thermal systems, easier service, and lower coordination load—are evaluated against collision cross-section, correlated loss, avoidance saturation, fragment yield, and rebuild burden.

The controller uses a mitigation hierarchy: prevent releases and explosions through reliability, passivation, containment and prompt disposal; avoid tracked objects through coordinated, uncertainty-aware screening and maneuver reserves; survive only the specified small-untracked-particle regime through shielding, placement, redundancy and leak isolation; compartmentalize consequences; then remove or recycle intact, massive, collision-likely derelicts. Shielding mass and increased cross-section are charged, and no practical shield is credited against a satellite-scale impact. Safe deorbit or relocation counts as hazard removal, not material recycling.

Shell-resolved triggers monitor active and derelict mass, conjunction forecast and uncertainty, maneuver workload and remaining propellant, disposal failures, fragment creation-to-clearance ratio, expected hazardous descendants, tracking quality, and service backlog. Crossing a threshold can slow or stop deployment, tighten the Eq. (27) cap, change planes or shells, increase spacing or fuel reserve, dispatch removal, isolate a cluster, or retire a shell. NASA’s mitigation guidance distinguishes creation prevention, small-debris protection, lower-risk orbital regimes, and collision avoidance; its conjunction handbook treats screening, risk assessment, maneuverability, tracking, reliability, disposal, and operator coordination as lifecycle functions [S65]. ESA’s 2025 environment report finds that mitigation compliance remains insufficient and that fragmentation can exceed natural clearance even without new launches, motivating active removal [S66]. These sources bound the control architecture; they do not calibrate a future million-node constellation or transfer Earth-orbit policy to LLO or NRHO.

The architecture search makes the failure domains concrete. Five declared 120-node layouts vary altitude dispersion, inclination, planes, along-track spacing, cluster cap, shells, gateways, control domains, shared power, navigation and software, and cross-link burden. The concentrated and plane-modular layouts violate the 10% common-cause budget at 100% and 25%; the multi-shell and sparse independent-domain layouts pass at 10% and 6.7%. A physically distributed layout with one gateway and two control domains still fails at 100%, demonstrating that orbital separation cannot compensate for a shared logical choke point. Download original CSV (3 KB) reports the collision/concentration/communications tradeoff and labels the non-dominated layouts rather than declaring one optimum.

The breakup diagnostic propagates a cloud through twelve individually specified nodes with altitude, inclination, plane, along-track phase, capacity, gateway, and control-domain identities. It reports direct loss, expected secondary collisions, avoidance maneuvers, service interruption, repair load, and restoration time. In the declared one-year stress cases, the 650-km Earth-orbit breakup generates 0.103 expected secondary collisions, 0.495 avoidance maneuvers, 72.7 capacity-days of interruption, and a 76-day 95% restoration time. The LLO case has weaker tracking, negligible natural clearance, and slower repair: 0.122 expected secondary collisions, 0.119 maneuvers, 117.4 capacity-days, and 149 days to restore. These are deterministic expected-count implications of an illustrative geometry and kernel, not integer event forecasts or catalog-calibrated collision probabilities. The full time series and summary are in Download original CSV (49 KB) and Download original CSV (715 B).

The high-conjunction stress separately removes tracking, communications, navigation, and centralized coordination. All five degraded cases breach the declared risk limit before intervention. The controller responds by pausing deployment, increasing spacing, switching to independent tracking and local safe mode, isolating control domains, and applying deterministic right-of-way rules as applicable; all cases fall below the limit only because the declared fallback multipliers are strong enough. That conditional result is visible in Download original CSV (2 KB) and is a test target, not evidence of operational safety.

The mitigation comparison crosses low/high deployment cadence, disposal reliability, removal, shielding mass, cluster cap, shell diversity, servicer fleet size, and repair/recycling capacity. Of 256 portfolios, 39 are non-dominated across residual risk, lifecycle cost, and delivered capacity. Download original CSV (28 KB) retains the full surface so a low risk point cannot be called universally optimal by hiding its mass, cost, or throughput penalty. Download original CSV (618 B) keeps Earth-orbit atmospheric clearance, tracking, station-keeping, residence, and controlled reentry distinct from LLO’s negligible atmospheric clearance, weaker tracking, higher station-keeping, and lunar-impact/transfer disposal.

Finally, shell admissibility is a shared governance constraint. The illustrative coordinated 5,200-node plan remains below the declared 10,954 node 650-km and 8,660 node LLO carrying-capacity limits and passes the 90% operator-compliance gate. The 15,000-node case exceeds both limits and also fails data-sharing, maneuver-coordination, disposal, and authorization requirements. Download original CSV (607 B) makes clear that one operator’s internal policy cannot authorize or coordinate the shared shell. All caps and workload coefficients remain ASSUMPTION-class pending catalog and operator telemetry.

One environment-specific case partly cuts the other way. For short-lived compute payloads in very low orbit, aligning useful life with accelerator-obsolescence cycles reduces the economic value of repair: hardware retired within a few years regardless costs less to be unable to fix. The qualifications are substantial. Natural decay depends on altitude, ballistic coefficient, and solar activity—small spacecraft near 400 km can decay within five years, but beyond 500 km five-year decay is not assured and some objects persist for decades. The leading published orbital-compute architecture places its cluster near 650 km in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, chosen for illumination rather than disposal [S32], so the concession does not describe that design. Nor is disposal free: station-keeping, collision avoidance (SpaceX reports more than 1,000 automated Starlink avoidance manoeuvres per day in 2025, Form S-1 pp. 9 and 153 [S27]), replacement launch, network spares, and residual capital loss all remain—and the same source that calls orbital repair impracticable proposes redundant provisioning instead, which is a cost, not its absence [S32]. The concession therefore covers some payload classes in very low orbit and does not generalize: mines, refineries, machine tools, and robots must last decades to close a loop. In these models it belongs in Part II (compute payloads), while Part I’s industrial δ\delta decomposition governs long-lived industrial equipment.

The clock-setting component. In any partially closed system, the component with the shortest replacement horizon that cannot yet be produced or stockpiled locally sets a hard clock on the entire complex. Closure priority follows failure rate × non-replaceability, not mass fraction. Viability requires:

Treplenish,j<Teffectivesurvival,jfor every critical component class j T_{\mathrm{replenish},j} < T_{\mathrm{effective\ survival},j} \qquad \text{for every critical component class } j

Canonical definitions and scoped units.

At low closure, nearly all equipment arrives from Earth. At intermediate closure, local industry supplies propellant, shielding, structural material, tanks, roads, landing pads, and simple machines. At high closure, the network also supplies motors, sensors, precision tools, computers, robots, spacecraft, factory machinery, high-purity chemicals, and semiconductor equipment. The progression is descriptive, not a scalar score: the identity and replaceability of the residual imports determine whether the system is actually autonomous.

The scalar form is vocabulary, not a measure of autonomy. A system supplying 99.9% of its mass locally is not autonomous if the residual 0.1% contains irreplaceable electronics. Yet that 99.9% can still reduce entry capital and Earth transport by orders of magnitude, support much larger deployed capacity per unit of external supply, and buy time in which the remaining process may be localized. Strict autonomy and import leverage must therefore be reported separately:

The deterministic support-policy stress test puts those metrics together instead of publishing mass closure alone. Its illustrative bridge has 99.86% commissioning-mass closure, 99.2% part-family closure, but only 72.8% purchase-value closure; both named residuals remain critical, so strict autonomy is zero in every row. The conditional entry architecture delivers a 2.5 t external seed rather than the 10 t wholly Earth-manufactured comparison; that 75% reduction is an ASSUMPTION, not a launch-cost estimate, and presupposes that the local bulk-material path already exists.

The large cumulative-loss entries are repeated waves of unsupported capacity, including capacity rebuilt and lost again; they are not fractions of one initial asset. The simulation serves replacement before expansion, applies input-specific shelf life, obsolescence, radiation-storage loss, failed-delivery derating, minimum lots, supplier caps, and synchronized replacement waves. It reports annual delivery mass, volume and value, inventory, replacement and commissioning demand, binding residual, and capacity loss in Download original CSV (30 KB); the companion Download original CSV (3 KB) keeps autonomy, mass, part-family, value, embodied-energy, process-work, entry mass, supplier utilization, runway, intervention, verification, and import leverage in one view. These coefficients are stress assumptions, not calibrated supplier or failure forecasts.

The disrupted case also charges 15% of otherwise available expansion effort to two discrete technical programs once their intelligence, embodiment, materials, tooling, and test-facility gates pass. The declared advanced-electronics program reaches its effort and development thresholds and validates a mature-controller route that reduces, but does not eliminate, its residual requirement; the calibration/metrology program reaches its threshold and fails. The 0.583 capacity-years spent on both programs are therefore unavailable for immediate expansion. Parent-tool ancestry, evidence state, charged work, minimum development time, and the probability-free success/failure outcome are explicit in the parameter file. Download original CSV (20 KB) allocates the consumed capacity-years across research compute, experiments, destructive tests, metrology, process equipment, prototype lines, qualification, failed designs, materials, and energy; the shares are assumption accounting, while the total is the expansion opportunity cost actually removed by the simulation. This scenario illustrates a possible path from scale to substitution without claiming that intelligence guarantees closure.

The external supplier is inside the hybrid system boundary rather than an unbounded input tap. Its factory throughput, high-purity materials, skilled labor-hours, energy, finance, and launch/transport capacity each grow at a declared rate; the minimum resource-equivalent flow, derated by supplier reliability, caps total deliveries before input-specific failed-delivery losses. Download original CSV (154 KB) reports every resource capacity, the binding supplier resource, delivered tonnes, and utilization in each year. This is still a stylized supplier envelope, but it prevents local growth from demanding residual imports faster than the modeled Earth loop can produce, finance, and transport them.

Finally, Download original CSV (2 KB) holds the capacity-proportional external-supply rule fixed and compares immediate expansion, a three-year replacement reserve, a balanced reserve/substitution policy, and substitution-first allocation. Substitution effort is removed from current expansion, while the stockpile policies withhold inventory from commissioning. That artifact reports maximum and terminal scale, stockout, external support, ending inventory, capacity loss, program effort, and validated or failed dependencies. It therefore shows when scale supplies useful substitution effort and when it merely enlarges exposure; no smooth automatic decline in import share is assumed.

The sector state is consequently an externally supported growth regime until the critical import vector vanishes:

𝑲t\mathbf K_t is the vector of commissioned sector capacities at elapsed year tt; 𝒚local\mathbf y^{\mathrm{local}} is locally produced capacity per year after internal material and service constraints; 𝒖t\mathbf u_t is the external input-flow vector; 𝑩\mathbf B converts imported inputs to commissioned capacity; 𝜹t\boldsymbol\delta_t is the sector loss-rate vector per year; and ⊙\odot denotes elementwise multiplication. This is hybrid expansion, not closure. It can nevertheless scale if a small external flow unlocks a much larger local material and energy base. Its ceiling, capital requirement, and resilience depend on supplier capacity, transport cadence, shelf life, stockpiles, substitution, and the minimum import cut sets—the smallest combinations whose loss collapses the network.

The path to autonomy is a sequence of verified substitutions, not an assumed trend: for each critical imported item the program must select a local process route, build its parent tools, qualify material and output, demonstrate yield and reliability, survive a supply interruption, and remove the import edge from the dependency graph. Intelligence can improve search and process development while the high-leverage external loop provides “fuel” for further expansion, but sufficient intelligence does not guarantee that geology, purity, equipment, energy, or safety requirements can be met within a horizon. The clock-setting component is the scalar shadow of this vector structure. The hardest closure problem is the deep technological stack—precision metrology, advanced electronics, semiconductor fabrication, optics, high-purity processing, specialized alloys, software verification, and the machines that make those machines (Part III.2 examines the first announced attempt on its terrestrial face).

Lineage. The 1980 NASA/ASEE summer study [S23] designed a proof-of-principle self-replicating lunar factory growing from a ~100-ton seed and introduced quantitative closure analysis; Freitas and Merkle catalogued the design space [S24]. The present thesis is that lineage plus three ingredients the 1980 study lacked: general-purpose AI for coordination and redesign; a reusable heavy-lift transport economy; mass-manufactured robotics.

The r and κ anchors, read honestly. Three quantities sometimes presented as converging near one year are not commensurable: solar energy payback (0.9–4.1 yr [S20]) measures energy self-financing only; the NASA ~1-year figure is a strawman replication target adopted for a proof-of-principle design, with component values its authors described as crude estimates; Gigafactory Shanghai’s ten months is project execution inside a mature host economy. The replication time of a full industrial ecosystem is unknown — and here it appears only as a computed output distribution (Part I.8). For κ, the honest headline is a theory-versus-demonstration gap, stated as its authors did: the 90–96% figure is closure reported in earlier studies of specific nonreplicating space-production applications, cited in support of plausibility arguments, and the 1980 study explicitly placed a rigorous demonstration that its factory could produce every required part beyond its own scope [S23]. Against that sit gram-per-hour oxygen and ~20% single-output yields actually demonstrated [S21]; full-system closure has not been demonstrated at any scale. Stating the gap converts the indicators of Part III.5 from rhetoric into measurable distance.

The seed-factory transition. Earth stops transporting finished infrastructure and transports a compact industrial seed, but “seed” denotes four inseparable layers:

  1. Physical seed: power, extraction, refining, manufacturing, robots, compute, repair capability, laboratories, and initial spares.
  2. Digital seed: AI weights, firmware, controllers, compilers, CAD/CAM, simulators, optimization and verification tools, and locally available software dependencies.
  3. Industrial memory: process recipes, material and equipment models, calibration and maintenance procedures, complete build records, failure histories, intervention traces, and provenance.
  4. Experimental capacity: instrumentation, metrology, test stands, flexible machine tools, and the ability to run controlled experiments that produce missing knowledge.

The package is viable only if it grows its productive base before critical imported components fail. A credible design requires redundancy, recycling, buffers, and an explicit path for every nonlocal dependency. No finite seed can encode “all necessary industrial knowledge”; the operational criterion is a sufficient foundation plus the capacity to diagnose gaps, run experiments, validate new processes, and incorporate the results into industrial memory. The ten-sector model represents only part of the physical layer: spares are a shelf-life-limited stockpile state; nonlocal dependencies are import lines that can be cut; and the “explicit path” is an abstract sector requirement matrix. The integrated layer sizes the seed and adds stylized representations of the remaining layers — a fixed 5 t digital-seed mass, task-coverage autonomy, intervention budgets, and commissioning dynamics (I.7, D.1). Those are declared proxies, not resolved requirements: collapsing storage, compute, calibration standards, laboratory machinery, consumables, and test articles into one constant means the model cannot yet determine which component of knowledge closure binds.

I.6 Intelligence, coordination, and time

A sufficiently capable AI converts much of organizational coordination from human management into a computational service: scheduling machines, allocating energy, routing materials, diagnosing failures, redesigning components, balancing inventories, planning construction, and proposing and coordinating candidate bottleneck-expansion projects. Observation, verification, materials, productive capacity, and authorization determine whether any proposal becomes operating hardware. A testable ASSUMPTION-class sensitivity form is

Raw agent count is not a coordination structure. EGE_G is derived from the active machine, software-agent, human-supervisor, supplier, regulator, and verification graph. Centralized, hierarchical, modular, sparse, and all-to-all organizations can therefore have the same number of agents and different burdens. Bandwidth, latency, context, embodiment, and verification limits constrain IeffI_{\mathrm{eff}} rather than disappearing into a generic model score.

Nor does greater task or coordination capability establish controllability. The authorized-capacity state in Equation (13) keeps task, coordination, evaluator, and controllability coordinates separate. It permits the first two to rise while independent evaluation or stop bandwidth binds, so a more productive system can simultaneously create a larger unauthorized-capacity gap.

A bottleneck is not relaxed when a design is merely proposed. For candidate upgrade pp, the accounting gate is

As intelligence and local autonomy improve, human management per unit of infrastructure can decline. The likely architecture is hierarchical rather than perfectly centralized: local controllers manage fast operations; facility-level agents coordinate production; higher-level planners allocate resources across the network.

An early terrestrial version is documented inside the same corporate ecosystem, though more weakly than some commentary claims. The confirmed systems provide real-time monitoring, production scheduling, quality management, and linked operational data at factory scale [S14–S17]. That is evidence that coordination functions traditionally mediated by human management are already becoming industrial data infrastructure. Claims that the systems replace management wholesale remain commentary-class and are not used here.

Coordination cannot reach zero. Machines must sense their environment; signals require propagation time; fabrication and motion take time; uncertain results require verification; and two projects cannot consume the same indivisible machine or stored resource simultaneously:

The limiting-case sweep makes the distinction visible. With one million declared model copies, compute can keep only 200,000 active; 40 machines, 25 experimental stations, and 20 independently verifiable work cells limit effective physical agents and annual physical output to 20. Another 6,500 instances can occupy declared simulation, planning, and monitoring tasks, while 993,480 copies wait or contend. A 12-step serial experiment chain at 0.1 year per physical result retains a 1.2-year floor; 1,000 independent experiments add four years on 25 parallel stations. Per-instance onboarding falls as copies share context, but aggregate onboarding, coordination edges, duplicate work, and verification demand rise. All counts are ASSUMPTION-class stress values. Machine-readable: Download original CSV (3 KB). The uncertainty comparison evaluates power, logarithmic-edge, and saturating-edge responses on the same reference case. It draws the irreducible floor, reference work, four elasticities, intelligence response, and saturation scale from declared bounds, using common draws across forms. No timestamped task-graph, handoff, delay, defect, supervisor, or verification telemetry is available, so this is a bound comparison with telemetry_status=unavailable, not a calibration. Download original CSV (514 KB) retains all 768 draws and Download original CSV (2 KB) reports p10/p50/p90 consequences. Median burden is 142.0 agent-hours for the power form, 141.5 for the logarithmic-edge form, and 149.3 for the saturating-edge form; the corresponding p10–p90 ranges overlap broadly. Structural-form uncertainty is therefore comparable to coefficient uncertainty in this one reference case, which is why no form is promoted.

The resulting burden enters one primary coordination-hours account. Schedule delay equals hours divided by declared staffing throughput; foregone verified output and failure probability are reported physical consequences. Lifecycle cost prices coordination labor only and does not also monetize the reported capacity loss. This one-way mapping connects schedule, capacity, reliability, and cost without charging the same burden under each label. Rehearsal telemetry must replace the assumption bounds before the relation is promoted.

After high closure the central allocation question changes from “can the system obtain land, permits, workers, components?” to “how much productive throughput should be assigned, and when will output be complete?”

When r exceeds δ, the idealized solution is exponential growth; real systems instead move through phases in which extraction, refining, power, thermal control, transport, precision manufacturing, compute, or maintenance is slowest. Intelligence accelerates growth by detecting and expanding that active bottleneck. The model below is an idealized, perfectly informed coordination benchmark, not a demonstration that an AI can observe, verify, and execute the allocation across a distributed factory. Within that benchmark, the co-binding set reported each step identifies the modeled active bottleneck.

I.7 The multisector model

The model that produces a real number needs, per critical sector, a capacity, a sector-specific depreciation, a requirement matrix, and import terms — with self-expansion defined as feasible positive net growth in every indispensable sector. The framework specifies it and the repository builds and runs it [S28]. Its elements:

  • Ten sectors: power, mining, refining, robotics, machine tools, electronics, thermal, transport, and — as first-class service sectors — repair and recycling. Repair offsets the wear component of δ only, at an efficiency cost and a spares bill drawn from the requirement matrix; recycling converts retiring capacity into secondary mining/refining feed, capped by the scrap flow.
  • Requirement matrix A[i,j]: units of sector-i output consumed to build one unit of sector-j capacity. ASSUMPTION-class, existing only inside named assumption sets (conservative / central / optimistic).
  • Decomposed δ per environment (I.4’s four components, per sector), assembled from anchored ranges where anchors exist and declared ASSUMPTION entries elsewhere. Retirement does not become fully recyclable scrap: environment- and loss-specific recovery factors distinguish wear, catastrophic loss, obsolescence, and logistics loss, and repaired wear is subtracted from retirement. Each resolved value carries a provenance record into the generated reports.
  • The allocation step: a three-stage lexicographic optimization. Stage 1 maximizes worst-case sector growth g over builds, wear repair, recycling, and stockpile drawdown. Stage 2 holds g at its optimum and minimizes normalized stock draw. Stage 3 holds both objectives and solves a strictly convex, normalized quadratic program over actions. This final tie-breaker makes the state transition unique instead of accepting an arbitrary LP vertex.
  • Strategic imported-part stockpiles with shelf life (electronics-class parts decay in storage), per-sector import cutoffs, Mars synodic pulse deliveries, and Poisson common-cause shocks hitting correlated sector groups (dust storms, solar storms, common design faults).
  • Three reference architectures: LEO (no ore body — feed imported or recycled from on-orbit mass), lunar surface (regolith feed, abrasive dust, no magnetosphere), Mars (deepest logistics penalty, ~26-month synodic resupply pulses, dust storms).

The electronics strategic-material gap. One structural parameter dominates the scoped scalar-anchor screen in I.8: the fraction of the electronics sector’s output mix producible off-world (sampled 0.10–0.30; ASSUMPTION with a documented bounding argument — advanced-node logic and memory are not locally closable in this scenario class; boards, passives, and power electronics plausibly are). No published measurement exists. Among the quantities currently parameterized, anchoring it is the highest-value observation this program could acquire; that ranking does not cover omitted structural uncertainties.

An AI accelerator is already a supply-chain assembly rather than a single “chip.” NVIDIA’s H100 specification separately reports 80 GB of HBM3, 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth, and 900 GB/s NVLink for the SXM product [S76]. TSMC separately describes front-end wafer fabrication and back-end advanced packaging, including CoWoS interposers; its 2025 annual report records qualification of a 5.5-reticle-size CoWoS solution and planned 2026 volume production [S77]. These primary-source quantities anchor the structural split, not the off-world coefficients.

The dedicated sensitivity resolves eight tiers: front-end logic fabrication, memory fabrication, advanced packaging, substrates/interposers, high-speed interconnect, power electronics, test/metrology, and radiation-qualified system integration. Each has its own shelf life, physical failure, economic-obsolescence, local production, import, reuse/down-bin, and shortfall account. The declared sequence localizes test/metrology, system integration/repair, and power electronics first; those three deliver more early fulfilled demand per illustrative localization effort than memory or front-end logic fabrication. The latter two retain a continuing Earth umbilical in this branch. This is a resilience sequence, not a claim that frontier fabrication is unnecessary. Machine-readable: Download original CSV (5 KB).

Integrated-bootstrap layer. The ten-sector model asks whether ten abstract capacities can grow together. The integrated model asks whether a declared physical seed can supply the material, service, autonomy, and commissioning requirements of another operating cell. It expands the graph to 18 sectors — separating interconnects/boards, passives/power, sensors/control, packaging/test, mature logic, advanced logic/memory, and process equipment/metrology — and 17 material categories (15 elements plus rare-earth and dopant classes; the model is material-category-resolved, not element-resolved — stoichiometric and process-chemical closure is not checked at the species level). Its material balance is

A material stock changes by recovered production, initial or external supply, and inbound transfers minus sector builds, losses, and outbound transfers. Every modeled element must balance across Earth, lunar, orbital, and asteroid arcs.

Canonical definitions and scoped units.

with explicit Earth→Moon strategic-material stock, asteroid→Moon feed, and Moon→orbit finished-compute arcs. The seed optimizer includes task coverage and residual intervention, construction lags, yield ramps, minimum viable scale, and process-specific gravity or centrifuge overhead. A dynamic pass then requires constructed capacity to ramp through commissioning before it contributes to the operating cell-equivalent aggregate. The equations, scenario definitions, and reproducibility record are in Appendix D and outputs/integrated/MANIFEST.md.

I.8 Results

Monte Carlo over anchored ranges with common-cause shocks (n = 400 sampled runs per cell; one shared draw per anchor per run, correlating parameter uncertainty across sectors; every replication time is an output). The state metrics are:

  • Balanced doubling (headline replication metric). λ(t) = min_j K_j(t)/K_j(0); balanced doubling occurs when λ ≥ 2 — every modeled sector has at least doubled in its own capacity units. This is a balanced-capacity event, not a claim that a complete commissioned second plant or physical seed exists. λ is invariant to each sector’s arbitrary capacity unit.
  • Aggregate doubling (secondary diagnostic). First passage of Σ_j K_j to 2× its initial value. This depends on the arbitrary units the sectors are denominated in and can be reached by overbuilding easy sectors while a hard sector lags and is therefore not the replication headline.
  • Endpoint hierarchy. Reported timestamps are step ends. (1) expanding@30 — realized post-shock worst-sector state change g > 0 at year 30, the weakest endpoint: such a run may still be import- and stock-supported; (2) pre-shock allocation endpoint — the optimizer’s intended g before shocks, retained as a diagnostic rather than the headline; (3) sustained — realized g > 0 at every step ending in years 25–30; (4) Earth-import cutoff — a separate central-set ensemble with all Earth imports cut at year 30, counting runs with realized g > 0 throughout 30–35 (stock draw permitted). In LEO, captured feed continues, so that row is labeled Earth import cutoff with continued capture feed, not autonomy. None of these frequencies is called a real-world probability.
  • Binding sector and co-binding. Each material-balance supply is relaxed by 1%, the allocation is re-solved, and the finite improvement in worst-case growth is measured. The perturbation is relative and therefore invariant to row units. Rows within 5% of the largest positive response form a co-binding set and share fractional credit. This replaces both the unit-sensitive slack heuristic and the degenerate LP-dual label.

The machine-readable outputs report two doubling denominators because they answer different questions: ever doubled is the first-passage time among all runs that ever reach the criterion within 35 yr (transient growth capacity); survivor-conditioned restricts to runs also expanding at year 30 (sustained expansion performance). Table 10 displays the ever-doubled denominator; survivor-conditioned counts and times remain in the CSV. The difference is a distinct outcome class — runs that doubled early and then lost viability. All shares are frequencies across this stipulated assumption ensemble and shock process — not empirical probabilities of real-world success (machine-readable table: Download original CSV (2 KB)):

Ten-sector model boundary. Every run starts with positive capacity in all ten sectors. This layer has no construction lag, commissioning, yield ramp, or minimum efficient plant scale, and it permits continuous fractional capacity. Its reported years are stylized first-passage times inside an already complete abstract seed, not engineering schedules for a transported factory. The separate integrated layer below adds a physical seed and commissioning dynamics, but remains assumption-class.

All doubling columns below are balanced capacity events (λ ≥ 2: every modeled sector doubled in its own units); the aggregate-metric columns live in the CSV. LEO rows describe the import/capture-supported orbital recycling network of I.6, not an autonomous ecology.

Reading: the conservative ensemble mostly fails on the realized endpoint: 3% of LEO, 8% of lunar, and 0.5% (2/400) of Mars runs are expanding at year 30. Central results are architecture-dependent: the realized endpoint is 67% in LEO, 56% on the Moon, and 15% on Mars, while only 31%, 5%, and 1% of all runs, respectively, remain positive throughout years 25–30. The gap between the pre-shock allocation endpoint and the realized endpoint is the cost of shocks at the reported step. The Mars synodic pulse can still flatter a single endpoint; λ = 0.55 and 4/400 sustained central runs show that contraction is the more informative reading there. Figure 1 exposes the full time path rather than privileging one endpoint.

Balanced doubling is faster on the Moon but the endpoint is more sustained in LEO: among runs that ever reach λ ≥ 2, the central median is 5.0 years on the Moon versus 26.0 in LEO. These are balanced-capacity first passages, not construction records for complete second factories. LEO has no ore body, so growth is throttled by captured and recovered material. Recycling yield is below unity and recovery depends on loss type; recycling alone cannot fund net expansion. The LEO Earth-import-cut row therefore preserves capture feed and must not be described as autonomy. The lunar surface has regolith feed and can grow quickly when electronics permits, while the finite-response diagnostic assigns about 96% of central lunar co-binding credit to electronics. The spread is the result: current evidence does not close feasibility, but the model identifies the conditional measurements that would.

Cut sets and the ensemble-frequent minimum cut. At central anchor values no import cut set is fatal by year 30 anywhere — imports accelerate but are not load-bearing at central values. That statement misleads alone, because cuts appear near the feasibility margin. Over sampled anchors (n = 40 draws per cell), conditional on an otherwise-expanding draw, central lunar electronics and the all-import cut coincide in this regeneration; central LEO is more exposed to the feed loop as a whole than to electronics alone; and the small central Mars survivor set produces no fatal candidate cut in this regeneration. Exact conditional frequencies have moved materially across equally valid small-n regenerations. They are reported in outputs/report_deep.md for reproducibility, but the defensible claim is ordinal: cut dependence appears near the feasibility margin and is architecture-specific; this experiment does not estimate a stable real-world probability. Capacity knockouts at central values: the eight physical production sectors (power, mining, refining, robotics, machine tools, electronics, thermal, transport) are knockout-indispensable in both architectures tested; repair is additionally indispensable on the lunar surface. With LEO’s 5% capture feed, a recycling knockout is survivable at central values. The structural point is: the LEO architecture lives on recovered and captured mass (capture/mining receives 98% of central co-binding credit), so its dependency is the feed loop as a whole rather than any single import line.

The clock-setting curve. Expansion frequency against the e-folding time of Earth-supply withdrawal (n = 60 per grid point; machine-readable: Download original CSV (314 B)): on the lunar surface under central assumptions, the realized year-30 endpoint is 0.40, 0.57, 0.43, 0.57, and 0.73 at 4-, 7-, 10-, 15-, and 25-year e-folding times. The non-monotonic wobble is within binomial noise at this n. The experiment is suggestive of a penalty for withdrawing the umbilical faster than the closure ramp, with electronics stockpile shelf life as a plausible mechanism. At n=60n=60 per point it does not estimate a stable response curve or its steepness; Figure 2 therefore preserves the observed sampling wobble.

Allocation-policy robustness. The results above could in principle be an artifact of the myopic one-step maximin allocator — a forward-looking operator might accept lower current worst-case growth to build future capacity. Because the dynamics and balances are linear, the finite-horizon LP is solved exactly — though receding-horizon control remains an approximation to full-horizon optimization (truncation and terminal-value effects persist; an investment paying off after year six is invisible to a six-year window). On paired draws (identical parameter samples per policy, shocks off), a six-year receding-horizon maximin reproduces the myopic policy essentially exactly — 16/30 vs 16/30 sampled runs expanding on the lunar surface, 11/30 vs 11/30 in LEO, with co-binding shares computed under the same finite 1% response definition as the baseline. The absolute level is not stable at this small paired n — the lunar count has swung across equally valid regenerations, so the policy equality is the stable finding, not the level. The agreement holds because the maximin criterion already directs each step’s investment at the worst-off sector, which is the future bottleneck. A third policy, maximizing aggregate growth subject to no sector shrinking, collapses (0/30 in both architectures): worst-case allocation is load-bearing, not incidental. Bottleneck-first heuristics are subsumed by the maximin construction itself. The defensible conclusion is correspondingly scoped: under paired, shock-free draws for the tested LEO and lunar central cases, a six-year receding horizon did not materially change the outcomes; global allocation-policy robustness (longer horizons, perfect foresight, robust control under shocks) is not established — and the retooling analysis of Part IV exhibits one regime where allocation family genuinely matters. (policies.py; paired-draw comparison in outputs/report_deep.md.)

Scalar-anchor sensitivity screening — with its scope stated. The claim that the strategic-material gap and logistics penalty dominate is a computation, not an assertion, and it is a scoped one — central assumptions, lunar architecture, shocks off, scalar anchors only; it does not rank structural requirement-matrix uncertainty, policy choices, shock distributions, or interaction effects, and repeating it across environments and sets with interaction-capable methods remains open cross-environment work: Spearman rank correlation between each anchor’s shared draw and the worst-case growth rate at year 30 across the ensemble (n = 300, central/ lunar, shocks off; anchors are drawn independently, so per-anchor rank correlation needs no independence corrections beyond the null band of roughly ±0.11, wider under multiplicity). Two parameters tower above the band: the space-electronics closure fraction (ρ ≈ +0.80) and the space logistics penalty (ρ ≈ −0.48) — both ASSUMPTION-class, which is the epistemic point: within this scalar screen, variation in year-30 growth is dominated by exactly the two numbers no one has measured. Every other screened anchor sits at or near the null band. (montecarlo.sensitivity; ranked table in outputs/report_deep.md.)

Integrated seed and aggregate-capacity results. The integrated layer is a second, explicitly assumption-class model, not a relabeling of the ten-sector balanced-capacity runs. Structurally it is a two-stage hybrid: a multisector, multi-material seed-sizing LP, followed by sector-resolved capacity-growth dynamics. All 18 sector capacities retain their own commissioning lag, ramp, and depreciation; the continuous operating-cell equivalent is derived as the slowest normalized operating sector rather than advanced as the state. The published central trajectory orders balanced seed-composition packets for continuity, while diagnostics compare independent maximin-sector, surplus-preserving, shock-aware, and perfect-foresight allocation. Failures enter explicit repair queues whose return to service consumes parts, repair service, intervention capacity, and time. Construction and commissioning are cohort-resolved. A scenario is LP-feasible when the seed LP admits a solution satisfying every material, service, autonomy, intervention, and throughput constraint over the scenario horizon. The doubling metric is first passage to two operating-cell equivalents — a continuous aggregate crossing, not a discretely commissioned second factory. The year-40 and terminal-window endpoints are separate. Central deterministic scenarios and deterministic 200-draw assumption ensembles:

The occupancy column is a count under the declared log-uniform sampling measure. It is not a calibrated probability, posterior, or empirical success rate.

“Minimum-mass installed seed” is the LP’s installed-equipment boundary, not delivered cargo. A separate deployment model adds packaging, unloading and site equipment, calibration references, initial spares, and startup-energy storage, then tracks delivered, staged, installed, commissioned, failed, recovered, and operating mass. Under those declared assumptions the 217.0 t lunar-bridge seed is 303.6 t delivered and reaches full operation at about 5.8 years. The LP result remains conditional rather than a global optimum over unknown processes or designs. A composition-changing Pareto search varies process route, redundancy, and source portfolio; its 36-point frontier is a design-space diagnostic, not a claim that the enumerated alternatives are exhaustive. The import-stock share is worth stating plainly: at 27% of installed mass, the central lunar bridge is a substantially Earth-provisioned seed whose local loop supplies bulk mass, not a nearly closed system with trace imports. The year-40 column carries the crossing-versus-retention distinction: neither the terrestrial rehearsal nor the lunar bridge ever reaches sector-balanced doubling in the 80-year extension, and their compute sectors fall to 0.47 and 0.54 equivalents at year 40. The Moon–asteroid case crosses two at 35.25 years and reaches 3.28 at year 40 while expanding. The strategic import stock’s composition is resolved in Download original CSV (2 KB): Ni, Cu, and C dominate at roughly 80% of the lunar-bridge stock, with initial-rate coverage near five years per category.

The strict lunar-only case is a structural infeasibility, not a sampled tail: the central LP is infeasible — the configured trace-material yields cannot supply the assumed electronics and process-equipment stack — and all 200 draws preserve that infeasibility, so 0/200 restates the structure rather than measuring an uncertainty. Substitution, a different electronics stack, a new refining route, or a richer measured deposit can change it; the result is not a proof that lunar-only industry is impossible. The Moon–asteroid case assumes a deliberately synthetic composite portfolio rather than a known accessible body: 187/200 states what a sufficiently diverse source network would have to supply, not that such a portfolio is accessible, jointly recoverable on the assumed timetable, or economical. In its central solution the Moon supplies 360.3 t/yr of feed and the asteroid portfolio 179.7 t/yr. Source occurrence [S51–S56] bounds plausibility; it does not validate recoverable yield, reserve, throughput, purity, or transfer cost. Figures 3 and 4 separate the installed-mass distributions from the resulting commissioning schedule.

Terminal-window, ablation, and frontier diagnostics. Five analysis passes interrogate the same declared architecture without introducing any new coefficient (machine-readable tables in outputs/integrated/tables/; all regenerate with rsi-run-integrated):

  • Sector resolution invalidates the scalar crossing result. The terrestrial and lunar-bridge cases are contracting (−0.022 and −0.027 equivalents over years 35–40), never cross two in the 80-year extension, and are bottlenecked by compute at year 40. The Moon–asteroid network crosses two at 35.25 years, reaches 3.28 at year 40, and is expanding (+1.323); advanced logic/memory is its slowest normalized sector. Machine-readable 40/60/80-year endpoints are in Download original CSV (912 B), and the full 18-sector state is in Download original CSV (917 KB).
  • The dynamic intelligence coupling is regime-dependent. The terrestrial and lunar-bridge cases are each material-limited in 145/160 quarterly steps, and separate freezes of research automation, task-autonomy improvement, and industrial-productivity improvement move their endpoints by less than 0.1%. The source-diverse network is material-limited in only 48/160 steps: removing both coupling channels reduces year-40 balanced capacity from 3.28 to 2.71, or 75% of baseline net growth. The 2×2 closure ablation supplies the stronger causal distinction: the bounded-controller, capital-reproducing branch still doubles at 36.75 years, whereas an active digital loop with every new-capacity order blocked never doubles. This does not validate the coefficients; it shows that the implemented feedback becomes operative only after the stipulated source vector relaxes material supply and that reproductive capital is a separate switch (Download original CSV (3 KB); Download original CSV (2 KB)). The starting AI level also binds statically: re-sizing at base autonomy makes the bridge and network seeds infeasible. The exhaustive primary-cap classification assigns the remaining 14, 15, and 112 steps respectively to the declared gross order-rate cap; live service capacity is never the primary dynamic cap (Download original CSV (323 B)).
  • The finite response to intelligence changes with complements. Holding every named complement fixed, a 0.1 capability-index uplift changes the terrestrial and lunar-bridge year-40 endpoints by −0.00016 and −0.00015 balanced units, respectively: both quotients are near zero while material binds in 90.6% of steps. In the declared Moon–asteroid network, the same perturbation raises the endpoint from 3.280 to 3.636 and advances doubling from 35.25 to 34.50 years, a local quotient of 3.560 capacity units per capability-index unit. The tiny negative values in the material-starved cases are numerical/path effects, not evidence that intelligence is intrinsically harmful. A separate upgrade registry prevents proposed designs from becoming free capacity: the illustrative metrology line pays 0.30 capacity-years and waits 1.25 years for design, 2.00 for construction, and 0.75 for verification before its increment appears at year 4; an underfunded radiator project never commissions. Light-speed latency, unavailable longitudinal observations, and external treaty authorization receive no automatic capacity increment (Download original CSV (3 KB); Download original CSV (4 KB); Download original CSV (15 KB)).
  • Scaling is not redesign. Installing scaled copies of the minimum-mass composition does not rescue the terrestrial or lunar bridge case by year 40. In the Moon–asteroid case, the 1.0×, 1.25×, 1.5×, and 2× seeds reach the first additional balanced equivalent at 35.25, 34.25, 33.5, and 32.5 years. This sweep does not choose a different sector mix.
  • Relabeling the LP objective is also not redesign. Lexicographic solutions for minimum installed mass, minimum Earth-import mass, and minimum intervention demand return the identical capacity vector in all three LP-feasible central scenarios. The current variables expose no tradeoff for those objectives to choose. A genuine Pareto front requires alternative process routes, redundancy, sector composition, or deployment decisions. The separate robust-seed search supplies those choices and reports dominated and non-dominated designs (Download original CSV (2 KB); Download original CSV (5 KB)).
  • Failure reasons and binding constraints are per-draw. Infeasible draws split between the autonomy threshold and the material LP (terrestrial 77/40, bridge 54/20, strict 33/167); feasible draws bind most often on Cu, C, Ni, and Cr (terrestrial and bridge) and on dopants plus refining and asteroid-transport throughput (network). The scalar-state claim that depreciation correlated positively with year-40 capacity is not retained: sector resolution makes depreciation and lag multipliers strongly negative against balanced year-40 capacity. The rank screen remains local to the declared independent multiplier measure, not a causal or global sensitivity result.
  • The strict-lunar cut is quantified. An elastic relaxation of the exact seed LP names the unsatisfiable rows and their minimum shortfalls over the horizon: Ni 19.0 t, Cu 18.4 t, C 15.3 t, Co 3.6 t, Cr 3.1 t, rare earths 2.3 t, Li 2.3 t, H 0.2 t, and dopants 0.1 t. The infeasibility is a distributed material cut, and the machine-readable infeasibility certificate doubles as the engineering target list any lunar-only architecture claim would have to defeat.

Figure 5 makes the limited timing benefit of scaling the unchanged seed composition visible.

The coupled run distinguishes installed compute from the slowest-sector industrial aggregate. Figure 6 compares those endogenous trajectories with rate-limited Earth-fed deployment. At year 40, the Moon–asteroid scenario has 5.11 normalized total endogenous compute capacity while its balanced aggregate is 3.28; compute is an independently constrained sector rather than a copy of the scalar cell count. The run exports 0.66 normalized units to orbit. Constant-rate Earth-fed orbital deployment reaches 1.56, 2.81, or 4.99 units under the tight, base, and responsive rate cases. Those curves show the difference between rate-limited deployment and endogenous capacity growth under the configured coefficients; they do not forecast datacenter capacity.

The stateful debris stress test reports the five-year fragment creation-to-clearance ratio RdebrisR_{\mathrm{debris}} — fragments created divided by fragments cleared over the final five years, a flow ratio rather than a branching-process reproduction number:

A ratio above one means only that more fragments were created than cleared in the window; it is not a cascade threshold. Strong mitigation lowers the dense case’s fragment index (3.18 → 1.69) and its flow ratio (4.40 → 3.97), but neither output establishes shell safety. The sparse case’s exact 1.00 is a zero-stock boundary, not a computed equilibrium,1 and appears only under an assumed 0.01 collision-kernel multiplier. The result supports topology as a co-designed industrial constraint; it does not establish a safe orbit, validate a debris environment model, or locate a cascade threshold. Complete tables and figures are generated from the same run in outputs/integrated/; Figure 7 shows the stock trajectories behind the windowed ratios.

What Part I establishes and does not. It establishes structure: which sector binds, what the minimum cut is, how locations differ qualitatively (lunar fastest-doubling but hostage to the electronics cut; LEO feed-constrained but recycling-viable; Mars most path-dependent and import-fragile, with no normalized scalar robustness ranking), and where the feasibility margin lies — structure that survives the allocation-policy variation above. The integrated layer additionally establishes which declared material, autonomy, gravity, source, and commissioning constraints explain its own seed scenarios. Neither establishes point feasibility: both requirement matrices, element recipes and yields, strategic-material gap, repair efficiencies, stockpiles, autonomy coefficients, lags, source portfolio, and shock/debris rates are ASSUMPTION-class. Solar-array, regolith, sample, or satellite data do not establish the coupled behavior of mines, bearings, machine tools, electronics production, or dust-exposed radiators.

  1. Realized clearance is capped by the fragments available. When the stock is empty, the reported creation-to-clearance ratio lands at its boundary value even though no positive-stock equilibrium has been demonstrated.↩︎

I.9 Development path, annotated

  1. Terrestrial autonomous-closure rehearsal. Before launch, operate an integrated seed factory on Earth using only the material forms, energy intermittency, communications constraints, spares allowance, and production methods intended for the lunar deployment. Exclude routine human entry; route every human intervention through a logged maintenance interface; inject equipment faults and communication outages; and require the system to manufacture, assemble, calibrate, and commission a second production cell. This stage does not reproduce lunar gravity, vacuum, radiation, or abrasive dust, so environmental qualification remains separate. It does test whether the industrial graph and its encoded operating knowledge are autonomous enough to export. Report intervention hours per machine-hour, imported mass per unit of added local capacity, critical bill-of-material lines producible, autonomous recovery fraction, time to a commissioned second cell, and every remaining single-point dependency. The execution contract in params/rehearsal_protocol.yaml fixes the boundary, typed event schema, ten binary gates, threat-complete fault campaign, 30-day retained-cell test, and parameter-replacement rules. Its generated matrix remains entirely execution_pending or data_pending; it is a protocol, not a result.
  2. Earth-dependent operations. Earth supplies vehicles, energy systems, consumables, spares, electronics, and nearly all machinery; space assets perform narrow missions.
  3. Local-resource supplementation. Local water, oxygen, shielding, construction feedstock, and selected propellant inputs reduce imported mass without yet closing the industrial loop.
  4. Heavy-industry closure. The network produces bulk metals, glass, ceramics, structural parts, tanks, simple mechanisms, roads, pads, and large power structures.
  5. Advanced-manufacturing closure. It adds motors, actuators, sensors, precision tools, robots, spacecraft subsystems, computers, and factory machinery. Terafab is best read as a terrestrial rehearsal of this stage (Part III.2): advanced-manufacturing integration practiced on Earth before any attempt to export it.
  6. Self-sustenance. Internal production replaces depreciation and failure across every mission-critical category; Earth supply becomes optional rather than load-bearing.
  7. Self-expansion. The system builds more mines, refineries, factories, power systems, robots, transports, and compute than replacement requires.
  8. Intelligence-industry recursion. Additional compute improves intelligence; improved intelligence raises industrial replication efficiency; higher output creates still more compute.

This is the implemented industrial branch of Equation (3): intelligence raises verified task coverage and replication efficiency; commissioned infrastructure adds usable compute; and that compute can support a further verified intelligence update.

The bridge economy maps onto the ladder: terrestrial products carry the early stages; launch and connectivity carry Stages 2–4; orbital compute is a candidate Stage 4–5 tread; and in-space industrial services carry Stages 5–6. The model adds stage warnings. The Stage 4→5 transition is where the strategic-material gap binds — no amount of Stage 3 bulk closure substitutes for an electronics tier. Stage 5 is location-dependent: LEO requires a sustained capture-and-recovery feed loop; under the present 5% capture assumption, recycling is valuable but not knockout-indispensable at central values. Mars requires electronics stockpiles engineered to synodic shelf life or a local electronics tier. The lunar surface has the fastest conditional balanced-doubling pathway when electronics closes sufficiently; LEO has the more sustained central endpoint under its continuing-capture assumption.

Location sequence and the lunar hybrid. The development ladder is not a ladder of orbital altitudes. In particular, Sun-synchronous orbit is a planet-centered orbit whose plane precesses to preserve approximately the same local solar time [S49]. The familiar dawn-dusk SSO is still LEO—the 650 km orbital-compute design assessed in Part II is an example—not the destination after a lunar surface base.

For closure, the more coherent topology is:

  1. LEO as a bridge, not the terminal reservoir. Communications, observation, early compute, assembly demonstrations, and transport can earn revenue and test systems, but bulk growth remains exposed to finite imported/captured feed and density-dependent collision risk.
  2. Lunar surface as the material backbone. Extraction, bulk refining, construction, durable storage, shielding, and long-life machinery use a physical foundation and local regolith. South-polar planning seeks the conjunction of long illumination intervals and access to shadowed volatile deposits, while leaving reserve size and extraction economics unresolved; dust and landing ejecta remain major surface penalties [S47].
  3. Sparse lunar/cislunar orbit as the service layer. Communications, navigation, observation, reusable transports, depots, assembly, and selected compute occupy orbit only where zero-g or illumination benefits repay shielding, stationkeeping, and service costs. NRHO is a candidate gateway geometry designed for eclipse avoidance and low stationkeeping, not a substitute ore body or a passive maintenance-free base [S48].
  4. Distributed heliocentric expansion after lunar export closure. Productive nodes then spread across separated Sun-orbiting trajectories and resource paths—potentially including near-Earth objects—rather than reproducing one dense shell. The point is diversity of orbital elements and feedstocks, not one privileged “solar orbit.” Moving inward raises solar flux but also heat-rejection, radiation, communications, and materials constraints, so no optimal solar radius is claimed.

Material-source sequence. The Moon is not chemically equivalent to Earth, but neither is it short of bulk machine-building elements. Its crust is dominated by oxygen, silicon, magnesium, iron, calcium, and aluminum, with smaller titanium-bearing and other phases; composition varies strongly between highlands and mare terrains [S51]. Those elements support oxygen, glass and ceramics, aluminum, iron-bearing alloys, silicon feed, shielding, structures, and many bulk machine parts, subject to extraction energy, purification, alloying, yield, and process-equipment constraints. The early system can therefore treat the lunar surface as a bulk-material backbone while importing low-mass, high-criticality material vitamins from Earth: advanced chips, dopants, catalysts, specialty chemicals, bearings, sensors, precision tools, metrology, and any alloying elements whose local recovery is not yet viable.

An order-of-magnitude inventory check prevents “no iron” from becoming a false premise. At an average regolith bulk density near 1.5 t/m³ [S52], one square kilometer excavated to one meter contains about 1.5 million tonnes of regolith. Applying the approximately 3 wt% iron reported for lunar highlands material [S53] gives roughly 45,000 tonnes of iron in place. This is an illustrative inventory, not an ore reserve: it says nothing about site homogeneity, mineral form, excavation losses, energy, recovery yield, environmental impact, economics, or how much is practically extractable. It does show why asteroid mining is not a prerequisite for initial lunar iron.

The harder question is diversity. Lunar carbon and nitrogen occur at low concentrations in returned fines, while polar water evidence remains spatially heterogeneous and does not yet provide a bankable reserve estimate [S54] [S55]. A robot-only ecology avoids agricultural and biosphere-scale demand, but it still uses volatiles and specialty elements for propellant, reduction chemistry, cooling, lubrication, polymers, process gases, electronics, and high-performance alloys. Carbonaceous asteroids and differentiated metal-rich bodies can eventually add water, carbon-bearing material, nickel, cobalt, and other feedstocks; returned Bennu material confirms carbon-rich organics and a history of water-related mineral chemistry in at least one carbonaceous body [S56]. Asteroids are therefore modeled as a follow-on route to diversity and supply sovereignty, not invoked as the first source of every machine metal.

Current demonstrations make individual conversion paths more concrete without closing the system. NASA describes integrated autonomous processing of regolith simulant into silicon solar cells, aluminum wire, oxygen, iron, and slag, alongside vacuum tests of molten-regolith electrolysis [S57]. These are meaningful subsystem demonstrations; they are not a lunar mine, an operational supply chain, a factory reproducing its own equipment, or an audited second production cell.

This ranks functions, not prestige destinations. Surface and orbit are complements: orbit is the transfer and service network; the surface supplies bulk matter and shielding. The ten-sector and Part II models cannot compare that hybrid directly: they isolate lunar-surface capacity, cislunar compute, and Earth-supplied lunar compute, and they aggregate elements into industries. The integrated layer adds material-category bills of material, source yields, Earth–Moon–orbit–asteroid arcs, and aggregate endogenous debris states. It therefore computes an explicit hybrid scenario, but its recipes, yields, transfer capacities, composite asteroid source, and collision kernels are declared assumptions. It does not establish lunar material sufficiency, a recoverable reserve, a launch date for asteroid supply, or an orbital safety case.

I.10 Binding bottlenecks and failure modes

With model annotations:

  • Lithography and fabrication equipment — the named residual chokepoint one layer below foundries, and the deepest single closure problem in this framework.
  • Reliability and repair — the model makes mean-time-to-repair and spares closure first-class: repair is an explicit sector with an efficiency and a spares bill.
  • Thermal management — radiators are launched mass; Part II’s radiator axis.
  • Energy storage and continuity — the lunar night storage mass term; Mars dust-storm shocks.
  • Resource quality — LEO has no ore body, so the sustained capture-and-recovery feed loop binds even though the separately modeled recycling sector is not knockout-indispensable at central values.
  • Verification and control — Part III.4.
  • Political and legal environment.
  • Economic survival of the transition — Part II.1.
  • Concentrated coordination — single points of failure a distributed competitor lacks.
  • Paradigm-shift stranding — Part IV.3; exposure concentrated in the fabrication layer, while the fleet self-insures through its own 3–6-year depreciation.

Part II — Comparative Economics

II.1 The bridge economy

Each stage of the recursion must be independently profitable or deliberately financed: a staircase of self-supporting steps, not a single leap to closure. The plausible treads, in order: terrestrial products of the same machinery (vehicles, storage, robots — the ground floor pays rent and turns the autonomous seed into an audited industrial experiment); launch and connectivity (Starlink revenue and launch services fund transport); orbital compute services — a candidate tread priced explicitly in II.2–II.4; and in-space industrial services at higher closure. The test of the staircase: at every stage, revenue plus strategic financing must exceed the burn required to reach the next stage before the clock-setting components of Part I.4 expire — and Part I.8 makes the clock concrete: the electronics stockpile shelf life against the import ramp. The commissioning trajectories in Figure 4 are the physical schedule that this bridge economy must finance.

Stage 0 has a second economic role. Building the candidate lunar industries first on Earth captures process knowledge, failure data, tool interfaces, simulation residuals, and commissioning procedures while the repair economy is still accessible. Selling terrestrial output can finance that learning, but the decisive deliverable is the measured ability to build and commission a second cell under lunar-palette and no-routine-entry constraints. A factory that is profitable yet requires tacit human rescue has not validated the exported loop.

II.2 The crossover model

Unit: dollars per frontier-equivalent kilowatt-year of delivered IT load — defined as one kilowatt-year of IT electrical load powering accelerators of frontier-generation efficiency, delivered at the case’s utilization; older-node capacity is converted by its J/FLOP penalty, so a frontier-equivalent kilowatt-year buys the same computational output regardless of which hardware generation supplies it. Three reference cases: a LEO inference service; high-orbit/cislunar batch compute; and Earth-supplied lunar-surface compute, with local manufacture entering only through the closure sweep. Mass and power budgets resolve from anchored ranges — launch price sheets (company_statement), flexible-array specific power and deployable-radiator specific mass (technical_report), accelerator system cost and lives (reporting), DC capex, PUE, WACC (reporting), qualification multiplier and utilization (ASSUMPTION, evidence-tempered) — each with a source class and per-run provenance. The space cost is affine in launch $/kg, so break-even launch prices are exact. Chip efficiency is a first-class parameter: off Earth, every watt not computed must be radiated, and radiator, PV, storage, and structure are launched mass, so a FLOPS/W advantage scales the entire power side per unit of delivered compute — efficiency and launch price enter the crossover multiplicatively, with a quantitative refinement below. This makes the popular framing of orbital compute as a launch-price race incomplete and supplies a thermodynamic rationale for internalizing chip design, not merely fabrication or supply security: the most efficient accelerator can tolerate a higher launch price because it carries less power and heat-rejection mass per useful computation.

Two lifecycle architectures are reported separately:

  • Integrated disposable satellite: compute, PV, radiator, storage, structure, and original launch spend retire together.
  • Serviceable/reusable platform: the compute payload refreshes on its hardware life while the power/thermal/structure platform and its original launch spend amortize over a longer infrastructure life. This is an explicit scenario assumption; modularity alone does not demonstrate serviceability.

The SpaceXAI economic thesis

The strongest documented case is broader than cheap solar. SpaceX defines cost per token as a function of the model, compute hardware, and energy. Its filings argue that near-continuous orbital solar can lower the energy term; radiative rejection can reduce cooling power; reusable launch, satellite mass production, and Starlink links can lower deployment and distribution costs; and faster access to power can put newer, more efficient chips into service before a terrestrial facility clears construction and interconnection queues. Proprietary chips and prospective vertical integration are meant to attack compute depreciation, which SpaceX itself calls the largest current cost-per-token component [S37] [S38] [S102].

That is a testable thesis, not a disclosed cost result. SpaceX tells the SEC that it does not publish a specific comparable cost-per-token figure, that the metric was not then used by management to evaluate performance or allocate resources, and that the filed comparison does not promise the industry’s lowest cost per token [S102]. The public record also lacks a fixed workload and quality boundary, full lifecycle bill, achieved AI1 availability and life, delivered communications goodput, and a commissioning/replacement record.

Musk supplied a separate dated prediction at the World Economic Forum on January 22, 2026: space would become the lowest-cost place to put AI “within two years, maybe three, three at the latest” [S103]. The comparison window is therefore January 22, 2028 through January 22, 2029. “Place to put AI” leaves the denominator ambiguous—it may mean marginal energy, installed compute, inference service, accepted output, or full lifecycle cost—so the statement is retained as a falsifiable comparison target, never as an engineering input.

Matching the denominator

The engineering reference remains 2026 USD per frontier-equivalent kW-year: it exposes spacecraft mass, qualification, life, replacement, availability, communications, and financing. The commercial translation is inference-only. It fixes one reference model, FP8 precision, batch 64, 1,024 input and 256 output tokens, a frozen held-out acceptance rule, and the same lifecycle boundary. For environment ee, accepted annual output is defined inline as Nacc,e=8760qreqnoutaQgeN_{\mathrm{acc},e}=8760q_{\mathrm{req}}n_{\mathrm{out}} a_Qg_e, and accepted-output cost as Cacc,e=106Ce/Nacc,eC_{\mathrm{acc},e}=10^6C_e/N_{\mathrm{acc},e}. Here qreqq_{\mathrm{req}} is raw fixed-workload requests per delivered kWh, noutn_{\mathrm{out}} is output tokens per request, aQa_Q is the held-out quality-pass fraction, and geg_e is the fraction delivered inside the latency, network, and service boundary. Training tokens and changes in model quality are excluded. Because CeC_e already divides by physical utilization, geg_e does not count physical uptime twice.

Time to useful compute and joint conditions

Ordinary WACC does not price the option value of earlier useful capacity. A separate schedule calculation therefore starts at January 22, 2026, applies a common 10% discount rate, and integrates accepted output through both forecast deadlines. The Earth scenario assumes two years for construction, interconnection, and commissioning followed by a six-month ramp. The company-only case preserves the possible-2028 deployment statement but returns not_computable because commissioning and useful-output ramp are undisclosed. The hybrid starts useful output on January 22, 2028 and assumes a nine-month ramp. Through January 22, 2029, it supplies 0.528 billion discounted accepted tokens per final kW versus Earth’s 0.710 billion, or 0.743×. Matching Earth’s dated output requires, one axis at a time, first useful output within about 1.79 years of the statement or a ramp below about 0.33 years. These are thresholds, not forecasts. The complete Download original CSV (2 KB) keeps every schedule class and missing value visible.
