No single launch-price, mass, utilization, communication, or goodput change in the registered range makes the hybrid cheaper on both denominators. An explicitly joint favorable corner—$0/kg launch, 5 kg/kW, 1.0× qualification, ten-year life, 0.99 utilization, zero communications capex, $20,000/kW hardware, 8% space WACC, full service goodput, first output in 1.75 years, and a three-month ramp—does reach 0.39× Earth LCO, 0.37× accepted-output cost, and 1.61× Earth’s discounted output by January 2029. That corner establishes genuine agreement: orbital solar and an extremely favorable integrated architecture can win. The present disagreement is over the simultaneous achievement of qualification, hardware cost, lifetime, availability, thermal-system mass, replacement, communications, and schedule—not over personalities and not over solar’s direction of effect.

A fourth, explicitly conditional SpaceXAI — AI1 disclosed design does not replace those references. SpaceX publishes a 150 kW peak / 120 kW average compute payload, 150 kW solar array, 70 kW/tonne vehicle efficiency, 110 m² liquid radiator, and deployed dimensions of 20 by 70 m [S38]. The model uses the array/average-load ratio of 1.25. Because the page does not say whether the 70 kW/tonne numerator is peak or average, aggregate vehicle mass is sampled over the derived 14.3–17.9 kg per average kW range and the direct disclosures retain company_statement provenance while the interpretation range is labeled ASSUMPTION. Radiator area, dimensions, redundant loops, shielding, and laser links are recorded but receive no invented mass or cost where none is disclosed. Hardware cost, qualification, life, achieved availability, and launch price retain the existing anchors.

The lifecycle split is explicit and assumption-class. AI1 publishes only aggregate vehicle mass, so the model first constructs the generic accelerator/PV/radiator/storage/structure mass budget and then scales every component by one common factor until its sum equals the sampled AI1 total. The resulting generic hardware-versus-infrastructure proportion assigns accelerator mass to the hardware refresh life and the balance to the infrastructure life in the serviceable case; the disposable case amortizes both on the hardware life. Capex is not inferred from vehicle mass: qualified generic accelerator capex is retained, while generic PV, radiator, and storage capex is evaluated at AI1’s disclosed 1.25 array-to-average-load ratio. The aspirational 10 kg/kW case uses the same proportional split. Neither that mass decomposition nor physical serviceability is disclosed by SpaceX; both are ASSUMPTION, and the serviceable AI1 and 0.76× boundary depend on them.

A fifth case is a deliberately optimistic, deterministic boundary rather than a new baseline: SpaceXAI — long-term targets plus favorable model assumptions. It uses SpaceX’s formal ≥99% launch-cost-reduction target as $185/kg and the prospectus’s long-term 100 kW/t orbital-compute scaling assumption (10 kg per average kW) [S37]. Because the company does not publish achieved AI1 qualification cost, useful life, or compute availability, the case separately labels as ASSUMPTION the favorable existing model bounds: 1.2× qualification, seven-year hardware life, and 0.95 utilization. It is excluded from Monte Carlo. Treating a target and three selected favorable bounds as probability distributions would manufacture a spurious probability of success.

Dated scenario policy. The named line is retained for the specificity of its public design inputs, not because SpaceXAI is the only orbital-AI program. As of July 28, 2026, the comparison class is publicly documented programs proposing or demonstrating space-based machine-learning or data-center compute, together with the launch, spacecraft, communications, and industrial capabilities of their named legal entities or disclosed partners. In that class, Google and Planet target two Project Suncatcher prototype satellites for early 2027 [S92]; Starcloud reports an H100 demonstrator launched in November 2025 [S93]; and Blue Origin’s Project Sunrise application was accepted for filing, not authorized or deployed [S94].

Every relevant model family therefore keeps the same ordered tracks: generic_reference, independent_reference, spacexai_disclosed_design, spacexai_stated_aspiration, and an affiliate hybrid only where a separately identified input is necessary. An independent result appears only when units and denominators match; otherwise the registry publishes not_parameterizable and the missing fields. The Download original CSV (9 KB), Download original CSV (43 KB), and Download original CSV (10 KB) preserve stable scenario identifiers, evidence classes, source snapshots, parameter completeness, actor boundaries, and the reasons a numerical line cannot be constructed. The disclosed design supplies six of the 24 full-lifecycle fields; the target case supplies nine only after its analyst-selected completion values are counted. No target, specification, or filing is represented as commissioned capacity.

Post-IPO architecture calibration. The technical literature available by late July 2026 does not supply one new “correct” mass-to-power ratio. It separates three architectures that should not be blended into one Monte Carlo distribution. Turyshev’s independent 1 MW high-sunlight closure allocates 29.4 kg/kW to PV, storage, and radiators; fixed spacecraft functions raise the total to 34–59 kg/kW [S39]. This independently brackets the model’s 46 kg/kW central generic LEO case and supports its order-of-magnitude placement, although the model’s full component-corner envelope (about 25–91 kg/kW) is wider. AI1’s derived 14.3–17.9 kg/kW sits below that conventional envelope and remains a separate company-specification case. Below both are research architectures: an integrated solar-compute-radiator panel concept at about 8.9 kg/kW and a tethered inference architecture at about 5 kg/kW [S40]. Those figures are legitimate lower-bound scenarios, but depend respectively on kilometer-scale integrated arrays, unqualified vapor chambers, thin tandem PV and custom ASICs, or on long tethers, distributed deployment, shielding, station-keeping, and micrometeoroid tolerance. They are pre-prototype architecture claims, not evidence that the generic spacecraft prior should move to 5–10 kg/kW.

Thermal closure is a system, not a radiator-panel coefficient. NASA’s flight and mission studies distinguish 2.75 kg/m² ISS radiator panels from 8.8 kg/m² after fluid loops and deployment are included; a JIMO study estimated 5 kg/m² for the complete system. At 353 K radiator temperature, 0.86 emissivity, and a 173 K environmental sink, the cited sizing is about 1.4 m²/kW, implying roughly 7–12 kg/kW for the complete heat-rejection system [S43]. This supports the middle and upper part of the model’s 3–12 kg/kW range, but shows that its low end represents advanced emitters, not a demonstrated full stack of cold plates, pumps, transport lines, deployment, and controls.

AI1 makes the ambiguity visible. Its published 110 m² radiator for 120 kW average compute is 0.92 m²/kW of quoted area [S38]. The one-face versus two-face convention alone moves the idealized surface-temperature result materially.2 The disclosure is not thermodynamically impossible, but its area convention, coolant temperature, and full thermal-system mass are crossover-critical unresolved measurements.

The terrestrial counterfactual responds — the epistemic requirement the static comparison missed. Three scenarios: tight prices scarcity (the politics-binds branch: permitting and climate commitments hold); base takes the anchors; responsive prices induced supply at the cheapest permitted firm-power floor — nuclear PPA, or the politically conditional natural-gas floor at $0.04–0.06/kWh (CCGT under $1,000/kW, ~2-year builds [S35]) — with an older-node hardware option taken when it wins on compute-normalized cost. Aspirational launch targets are sweep axes except in the explicitly labeled deterministic best case above; they never enter the probabilistic baseline.

Starship V3/V4 aspiration, normalized. SpaceX’s June 2026 prospectus does not quote a V3 or V4 customer price or a vehicle-specific cost per flight. It states instead that fully reusable V3 is designed to carry 100 metric tonnes to orbit, that a future generation could reach 200 tonnes as soon as V4, and that mature Starship is intended to reduce the historical $18,500/kg cost benchmark by 99% or more [S37]. Exactly 99% implies $185/kg; “or more” implies a lower value. Table 18 converts that formal aspiration and three more aggressive sensitivity cases into full-payload flight-cost equivalents:

Table 18. Mature-Starship launch-cost sensitivity axes and full-load equivalents.
LEO sensitivity case $/kg V3: 100 t full-load equivalent V4: 200 t full-load equivalent status
formal corporate aspiration ≤$185 ≤$18.5M ≤$37M derived from the stated ≥99% reduction; not a price quote
aggressive mature-Starship case $100 $10M $20M scenario axis
extreme fuel-like case $50 $5M $10M scenario axis
extreme lower case $30 $3M $6M scenario axis

The dollar-per-flight columns are arithmetic ($/kg × full payload), not company forecasts.3 Under-filled flights cost more per delivered kilogram; external customer prices can exceed internal marginal cost; and none of these figures includes a demonstrated cadence, reuse count, refurbishment burden, or capital-recovery schedule. This analysis therefore uses $185/kg as the traceable corporate aspiration, $100/kg as an aggressive case, and $30–50/kg only as an extreme fuel-like sensitivity band. All remain comparison axes; $185/kg also enters the quarantined deterministic best case, never the Monte Carlo.

Two financing caveats are deliberate modeling choices. Earth uses an 8–15% WACC range and space a separate 10–22% range. Qualification multiplier, service life, repairability, and utilization are still sampled as separate anchored quantities; the favorable corner likely has correlated engineering causes, so its deterministic result is a boundary rather than a joint probability claim. Calibration: the Earth base case works out to ≈$1.7/kWh, matching published accelerator rental rates.

Cost accounting — included and excluded. Included: IT hardware with qualification premium; PV, radiators, storage, structure and their launched mass (with cislunar/lunar delivery multipliers); pumping power, rejection temperature, chip-to-radiator temperature drop, environmental view factor, and a thermal-reliability mass margin; spacecraft bus, communications, ground network, program NRE, insurance, spectrum/regulatory cost, disposal, and residual value; capital recovery at the architecture-specific WACC with component-specific lives; compute-hardware replacement and its launch mass on the refresh cycle; an operations fraction for ongoing ground segment, downlink, and station-keeping; utilization derating; Earth-side DC capex, PUE, hardware refresh, and firm-power floors. Excluded: launch-site, landing, turnaround, and fleet infrastructure beyond whatever is implicit in the $/kg target; launch failure beyond the insurance proxy; collision externalities and constellation-replenishment logistics; tax treatment; and architecture-specific link budgets or regulatory outcomes. Turyshev’s independent inequality remains a useful cross-check: at 40 kg/kW, a terrestrial infrastructure allowance of $10,000–40,000/kW permits only $250–1,000/kg for launch and spacecraft build combined before communications, operations, utilization, and finite-life penalties [S39]. The net direction of the remaining exclusions is not claimed to be uniformly conservative. The reported multiples are stylized-architecture outputs with wide ASSUMPTION ranges; the robust conclusion is structural — which terms dominate — not the exact ratios.

All sixteen architecture/reference rows have zero sampled points below parity in 2,000 draws. This is a design-space statement under the declared sampling measure, not a confidence bound on real-world success. Figure 9 shows the separation from parity across the sampled cells without assigning real-world probabilities to them.

AI1’s aggregate mass disclosure is material but not sufficient at the retained central values: it cuts launched mass from about 54 to 16 kg/kW and LCO from about $77,600 to $46,500/kW-yr, yet fixed non-launch costs still exceed Earth base (central break-even approximately −$3,460/kg). With the remaining anchors simultaneously favorable — qualification ×1.2, seven-year life, and 0.95 utilization — AI1 is 1.74× Earth at the central launch anchor, has no positive break-even launch price (approximately −$191/kg), and reaches 1.13× at $250/kg. Completing communications, bus, NRE, insurance, spectrum, disposal, thermal-margin, and financing terms leaves no favorable-corner crossover at these assumptions.

The aspirational case makes that conditionality explicit. The two company numbers alone—$185/kg and 100 kW/t—still produce about $34,200/kW-yr, 2.33× Earth base when qualification, life, and utilization remain at their central values. Selecting the three favorable non-company bounds as well produces about $16,000/kW-yr, 1.09× Earth base. The incomplete-cost boundary produces 0.76×; including the omitted system terms reverses that result. All five favorable conditions must hold together, and the model assigns no probability to them.

The company’s own scale target exposes the feasibility burden. At 100 GW deployed annually and 100 kW/t, the flow is one million tonnes/year: 10,000 full 100-t V3 launches (27.4/day), or 5,000 full 200-t V4 launches (13.7/day), and roughly 833,000 AI1-sized 120-kW-average spacecraft. Even at $185/kg, launch cost alone is $185 billion/year before spacecraft manufacture. At the later AI1 page’s disclosed 70 kW/t, the same flow rises to 1.43 million tonnes and 14,286 full V3 launches/year. The current design is therefore 30% below the older 100 kW/t assumption; reaching it requires 43% more kW/t. Full rapid reuse, daily turnaround at unprecedented cadence, upper-stage recovery, fleet size, range capacity, and manufacturing are load-bearing. So are seven-year whole-system reliability and 95% compute utilization, neither published for AI1. Collision externalities, constellation replenishment logistics, and landing/turnaround infrastructure remain excluded, while terrestrial energy, chips, cooling, permitting, and construction can also improve. The prospectus itself identifies approvals and spectrum as dependencies and warns that better terrestrial energy could reduce the orbital advantage [S37].

The lifetime interpretation is architecture-dependent. The model’s 10–25-year infrastructure life is defensible only if the power and thermal platform survives multiple accelerator generations and the compute payload can actually be exchanged, serviced, or economically separated. For an integrated, non-serviceable LEO vehicle, the relevant infrastructure life is instead close to the spacecraft or compute life—typically about five years in the studies reviewed here [S39–S42]. The serviceable-platform and integrated-disposable results above expose both lifecycle readings. Shortening every component to five years is appropriate for an integrated vehicle, but too pessimistic once modular payload replacement is demonstrated. Platform reuse is a named architecture gate, not an innocuous amortization choice.

A negative break-even means fixed, non-launch costs alone exceed the Earth cost: at those draws no launch price, even zero, closes the gap. The structural finding: the crossover is gated by the space-qualification premium, equipment life, and utilization — not launch price alone. The generic-LEO crossover surface (launch $/kg × life × qualification × radiator × closure × chip efficiency) shows no ratio-below-1 region at published prices on any single axis, and near-parity only in the defined Starship aspiration cases ($185/kg formal; $100/kg aggressive; $30–50/kg extreme) combined with favorable values on at least two other axes. AI1’s disclosed aggregate mass is a multi-parameter architecture constraint rather than a single-axis point on that generic surface; it produces the conditional near-published break-even above while leaving no competitive draw in either lifecycle ensemble. At the central LEO architecture’s approximately 54 kg/kW, those prices correspond to initial launch expenditures of about $9,990, $5,400, $2,700, and $1,620 per installed IT kW, respectively, before annualization. They largely remove the current launch bill, but a negative break-even still means they cannot overcome the fixed qualification/life/utilization gap on their own. Lunar closure is the weakest lever: chips are never closed, so even 95% closure of non-chip mass leaves the lunar case roughly 15–30× Earth at published prices — still more than an order of magnitude from parity. Figure 10 displays the five one-axis sweeps on a common logarithmic cost-ratio scale.

The mass-multiplier refinement: at anchored values a 2× FLOPS/W advantage buys about 50% of the benefit of halving launch price (ratio 5.1 vs 4.2 at $3,000/kg, both from 6.1), because the hardware term — untouched by efficiency — dominates both mass and capex. “The compute tax outweighs the launch tax” [S34] becomes true only after the qualification premium and hardware $/kW fall; near-term, both taxes are subordinate to qualification and life.

II.4 External claim and independent-study checks

The public crossover claims are recorded as comparison targets (never inputs). The completed-cost model does not reproduce the stronger Google/Planet crossover claim, even at its favorable anchored corner; this converts the disagreement into an architecture- and accounting-wide, testable one. The post-IPO review of independent studies below then checks the model rather than merely restating corporate claims. The Suncatcher design study does not claim system-level parity. Its cost section states twice that it is not a full economic analysis and not a comprehensive economic feasibility study, and its comparison sets the amortised launch component alone (≈$810/kW-yr for a Starlink-v2-class mass-to-power ratio at $200/kg; $810–7,500 across satellite classes) beside terrestrial data-center electricity spend (≈$570–3,000/kW-yr), explicitly excluding infrastructure, building, and chip costs [S32]. That is a launch-cost feasibility marker — the finding that launch need not remain independently prohibitive — not a parity claim, and it is consistent with this model, which reproduces launch as a minor term. The crossover claim this model contradicts is the stronger reading in circulation [S34], not the study’s own.

  • The Google/Planet study (reported: crossover at $200–300/kg [S34]). At $250/kg with central anchors: space/Earth = 2.61 — no crossover. Under the favorable corner within anchored ranges (qualification ×1.2, 7-year life, 0.95 utilization, 3 kg/kW radiators): 1.26 — still no crossover. The disagreement is no longer localized to launch price or three performance inputs; the completed non-launch system boundary is load-bearing.
  • The Suncatcher design study [S32] describes an 81-satellite dawn-dusk sun-synchronous cluster near 650 km with terabit-class optical links (an 800 Gbps unidirectional bench demonstration against a stated ~10 Tbps per-link requirement) and a learning-curve projection of ≲$200/kg by the mid-2030s — itself conditional on roughly 370,000 tonnes of additional cumulative mass launched, on the order of 1,800 Starship-class flights averaging ~180 per year, which the authors call ambitious. Its engineering results should be read precisely (arXiv v2, 17 June 2026):
    • HBM was the most TID-sensitive subsystem — irregularities from ~2 krad(Si) against a ~750 rad(Si) shielded five-year requirement, with no hard total-dose failures to 15 krad(Si) — while core logic and on-chip SRAM were the most SEE-sensitive. The reported inference error probability is roughly one per three million inferences under the stated assumptions, with the effect on training explicitly reserved.
    • At ~150 rad(Si)/yr, a seven-year dose (~1.05 krad) sits below the ~2 krad irregularity onset — the radiation results support five-year TID survivability with margin and do not obviously contradict seven-year TID survival.
    • What they do not establish is seven-year system reliability: SEE-induced corruption, host interruptions, training sensitivity, thermal management, and whole-spacecraft failure remain unresolved, with orbital repair called impracticable and redundant provisioning proposed instead — a cost, not an absence of one. The COTS practice supporting a low qualification premium (unmodified accelerators flying on imaging satellites [S34]) demonstrates cheapness, not five-year reliability.

The independent checks localize four additional gates:

  • Conventional mass and economic closure. Turyshev closes PV, eclipse reserve, thermal rejection, fixed spacecraft functions, sustained communication, utilization, and finite life in a single framework [S39]. Its 34–59 kg/kW total independently brackets and supports the generic central mass at the order-of-magnitude level. Its more important result is the combined launch-plus-build ceiling: $250–1,000/kg at 40 kg/kW before communications and lifecycle penalties. Every additional $1,000/kW of communication or operations cost reduces that allowance by $25/kg. Current public launch prices consume more than the entire allowance before a spacecraft is built.
  • Low-mass architectures are conditional, not contradictory. The integrated-panel and tether studies reach 8.9 and roughly 5 kg/kW respectively [S40], demonstrating that mass is an architecture variable rather than a universal constant. Both target inference and both exchange conventional subsystem maturity for deployment, structural, thermal, and custom-silicon risk. They justify explicit stretch scenarios; they do not justify assigning conventional spacecraft a five-kilogram prior.
  • Inference and training are different products. Van Berkel compares a terrestrial 8,000-accelerator Clos fabric with orbital meshes: about 28,800 TB/s of terrestrial bisection bandwidth versus approximately 2.25 TB/s for a two-dimensional and 10 TB/s for a three-dimensional orbital mesh at 100 Gbps links, with network latency 150–450 times higher [S41]. Even much faster optical links do not remove multi-hop diameter and collective-communication latency. The appropriate early comparison is therefore per-satellite or loosely coupled inference, preprocessing, and communication-integrated edge work—not frontier distributed training. Training should receive a network-performance model, not an ordinary utilization scalar.
  • Small space-native nodes already have a different cost structure. The peer-reviewed HPCA microdatacenter study finds power and thermal systems dominate bespoke small-satellite TCO, while compute hardware can be less than one percent; energy-efficiency improvements can reduce TCO by about two-thirds and are up to 2.5 times more valuable in space [S42]. This is encouraging for 0.5–10 kW Earth-observation preprocessing, where data originates in orbit and downlink is avoided. It is not evidence that a megawatt terrestrial-substitution service has the same economics.

The broader policy cross-check reaches the same conditional result by a different route. A University of Virginia assessment reports a simplified five-year 1 GW case at $135.6 billion in orbit versus $16.6 billion on Earth under present-style assumptions; near-parity appears only when launch falls to $30/kg, satellite hardware to $10/W, specific power rises to 100 W/kg, sunlight availability to 80%, and degradation and GPU failure both fall to 1% [S44]. Its model omits GPU cost, financing, insurance, logistics, and downtime and should not be treated as a precise forecast. Its contribution is the joint-condition result: parity emerges from several simultaneous improvements, not from launch price alone.

Consequence for the staircase, stated within the model’s service definition: the modeled orbital architectures are not cost-competitive as substitutes for terrestrial frontier compute at the stated assumptions. That conclusion has a workload boundary: it applies directly to per-node inference in the cost model, while the cited network evidence makes frontier distributed training less favorable than the scalar model shows. It does not price differentiated orbital products (in-orbit sensor processing, sovereign or military demand, resilience niches), which could be profitable while losing the commodity comparison. What follows for the staircase is correspondingly bounded: commodity-scale deployment ahead of the enabling corner is strategic positioning or learning investment rather than substitute-compute profit — an observation Part III converts into a discriminating test.

The electrical comparison is also reported in workload-specific units so a kW-year is not silently treated as equivalent computational output:

II.5 Competition and milestone order

A one-dimensional “takeoff speed” label hides the relative order of digital, embodied, capital, and control milestones. The branch screen therefore crosses fast/slow digital progress with fast/slow physical closure. Its years are named ASSUMPTION coordinates, not forecasts:

Table 22. Milestone order under fast and slow digital and physical progress branches. Download original CSV (3 KB).
branch TAIR&DT_{\mathrm{AIR\&D}} TembT_{\mathrm{emb}} Tcl,ET_{\mathrm{cl},E} Tcl,ST_{\mathrm{cl},S} consequence
fast digital / slow physical 4 12 16 26 eight-year intelligence overhang before embodiment; off-world closure is post-AI construction

fast digital / fast physical 4 5 7 9 both loops advance, but Earth still closes first

Fast digital progress does not remove experiment, actuator, factory, material, deployment, or commissioning latency. It creates an intelligence overhang whose useful product is limited by those complementary stocks. Conversely, fast physical closure can compound with a bounded controller. The article’s off-world pathway is strategically causal rather than solely a post-AI construction program only in orderings where off-world closure changes the growth path before TAIR&DT_{\mathrm{AIR\&D}}; the sufficient screen used here is Tcl,S<TAIR&DT_{\mathrm{cl},S}<T_{\mathrm{AIR\&D}}. The matrix does not assign that ordering a probability.

The fast-digital/slow-physical branch is a stress test against AI 2027, not a copy of its calendar [S80]. That source explicitly focuses on a software-driven feedback loop because improved hardware takes longer to produce at scale, distinguishes coding execution from research taste, and publishes wide uncertainty. Its site later corrected a plotted trajectory and moved a median back while retaining a fast branch. Versioning is therefore substantive: no date or compute allocation from that scenario enters this model. [S35] supplies a separate fast-takeoff and capital-mobilization countercase under its existing source entry. Its ordering permits AI-R&D automation to precede broad robotics; the article’s embodied-closure path instead asks when physical tasks and capital reproduction pass their own gates. Amodei’s complement taxonomy [S79] explains why both can be coherent: digital capability may move first while hardware, data, experiments, human constraints, and physical law continue to set the realized rate.

A fifth branch makes the terrestrial counterfactual explicit. Powerful AI first accelerates terrestrial robotics, fabs, power, and launch supply; the illustrative screen closes Earth at year 10 and space at year 18 while reducing the off-world bridge-cost index to 0.65. Lower bridge cost helps space, but earlier Earth compounding raises the benchmark it must beat. Machine-readable: Download original CSV (3 KB). The fast AI-R&D countercase remains represented by [S35], without treating its calendar as established.

The system is not alone. China is the closest existing implementation of the terrestrial stages at national scale (solar, batteries, robotics, rare-earth refining, trailing-edge fabrication) lacking, for now, a reusable heavy-lift economy. Hyperscalers close the same inputs with capital rather than ownership — power agreements, custom silicon, supply contracts — which works until aggregate demand outruns what markets can scale. State programs hold ISRU roadmaps but iterate slowly.

Two corrections to the launch-chokepoint assumption, both cutting against a durable launch monopoly: payload cost-performance improved by two to three orders of magnitude over the decade against a smaller multiple for launch price [S34] — a crossover model treating launch as the primary axis mis-weights its own sensitivity analysis (borne out in II.3, where the crossover is not launch-gated); and chemical rockets are a local optimum — mass-manufactured vehicles, electromagnetic or kinetic launch, and mass drivers from a low-gravity surface (named in the fabrication initiative’s own material [S29]) would reset the launch axis rather than move along it.

Externally induced supply versus internally controlled reproduction. Expansion purchased through markets can pay stacked scarcity rents when demand outruns supply. Properly qualified: markets are not static — the right formulation is a race between demand growth and induced supply with multi-year capacity lags as the binding term, and whether internal replication beats inducing market expansion is a rate comparison (which is what the responsive counterfactual of II.2 implements on the power axis). A self-replicating base escapes mandatory dependence on external Earth markets — not economic allocation, opportunity cost, or internal pricing, which persist in any multi-firm or internally-priced closed ecology: expansion re-denominates from currency into materials, energy, and time. Two caveats: the entry ticket is still paid in dollars — the first self-replicating unit is bought, not grown, which is what the bridge economy exists to finance — and the logic predicts convergence, not uniqueness: every serious actor eventually verticalizes or plateaus; the durable advantage is the shortest hardware doubling time once everyone is. Historical reference classes calibrate “unprecedented”: Manhattan and Apollo peaked near 0.4% of GDP; British railway investment ran ~40% of GDP over a decade; wartime borrowing far exceeded either [S35]. Trillion-scale buildout is extreme but inside the envelope. The relevant question is therefore the relative rate, financing, and dependency structure—not escape from capital itself. The symmetric dynamic diagnostic gives both Earth and space endogenous investment and finds that physical space compounding does not become self-financing in either declared 40-year case.

Integration versus modularity (the Coasean resolution). Markets scaled semiconductors a billionfold through disintegration; why would this time differ? A firm’s boundary sits where internal coordination costs exceed market transaction costs [S25]. AI attacks the internal term (Part I.6) — but it attacks the external one too, improving supplier discovery, specification, contracting, monitoring, quality assurance, pricing, logistics, and modular interface design. The correct conditional is therefore that AI moves the efficient boundary toward integration only if it reduces internal coordination costs faster than it reduces interfirm transaction costs, an empirical question this document does not settle; what does survive is that the market interface retains an irreducible capital requirement efficiency gains do not remove. The defensible conclusion is bounded: AI may move the efficient boundary toward integration — not that ownership integration outperforms modular ecosystems in general. Three qualifications are central: markets also supply experimentation, selection, redundancy, and price signals, which an integrated complex must replicate internally or decay into soft-budget pathologies; technical closure (the network can produce its inputs) must not be conflated with contractual or ownership closure — this thesis requires only the first; and the in-domain integration success story confounds integration with reusability, cadence, and incentives [S1].

The operating wall. Physics-priced inputs (energy, materials, machine-hours) fall with scale; society-priced inputs (land, permits, interconnection, litigation, goodwill) rise with it — on Earth, closure has a structural ceiling because land, law, and neighbors cannot be internalized. Space shrinks and relocates the society-priced term rather than abolishing it, with one favorable property: permission attaches to the gateway (launches, spectrum) rather than the complex, so the millionth robot needs no new municipal permit. The hard physical version: Earth has a planetary waste-heat budget; space offers radiator area not bounded by a planetary surface (though still bounded by matter, transport, geometry, and maintenance — Part IV) — though not free rejection. Two external observations bracket how hard the wall binds now: data-center siting is already politically contested over electricity, water, and land — the society-priced curve observed from inside the industry [S34] — while the AGI-buildout literature meets the same wall with natural gas and deregulation at a firm-power floor below the nuclear PPA, never mentioning orbit [S35]. The wall binds through politics more than physics or long-run capital — though near-term hardware (turbines, transformers, cooling, construction capacity) can also bind — and the difference between branches is a parameter in this model, not a mood. And the sequence remains brutal: before high closure, space is the most expensive place to operate — every kilogram of spares travels at full launch freight while depreciation runs at its worst (II.3’s ~4–9×) — so the declining-cost regime switches on only after κ is high, which is why the bridge economy and the clock-setting components decide who survives to reach it.

The threshold-model argument. If RSI capability is a threshold — a base model good enough to run verified improvement loops — a smarter starting model confers a head start that the loop erodes; the durable variable becomes who runs more loops, which is hardware. Mid-2026 evidence supports continued benchmark compression between open and proprietary models (open-weight releases benchmarking near the frontier [S12]); it does not establish commoditization at an autonomous-R&D threshold, so hardware dominance is the small-α branch of the model rather than the established trajectory. If RSI-grade capability does arrive in open weights, model advantage weakens sharply without evaporating — post-training, proprietary data, evaluation systems, inference infrastructure, tool integration, operational reliability, distribution, and the capacity to run physical experiments all persist as differentiators — and to that extent the contest shifts onto the physical loop, the strongest form of the verticalization thesis. The counterpoint: the argument holds only if capability is threshold-like rather than continuously compounding (L_RSI ∝ Aα·Cβ·V^γ, with α unknown); benchmark convergence does not establish that autonomous R&D capability is threshold-like. And the structural counterweight: models converge because they train on the same public data, so residual differentiation concentrates exactly in proprietary physical-process data (Part I.2) — if general capability commoditizes, the model contest narrows to the domains where training data is generated by owned industry, folding the model race back into the physical loop.

Part III — Strategy Interpretation and Governance

III.1 A Musk-associated technology stack

The following mapping is an analytical interpretation of how existing companies could supply layers of the proposed system — not proof that they are managed as one program, although the 2026 developments (the Terafab initiative; SpaceX’s absorption of xAI) bind the transport, communications, intelligence, and fabrication layers by overlapping control, strategic coordination, and contractual collaboration. Tesla remains a separate public company; a shared controlling figure and a framework agreement are not common ownership (Form S-1 pp. 7, 10, 154) [S27].

The dated comparative claim. As of July 28, 2026, and within the comparison class of publicly documented programs proposing or demonstrating space-based machine-learning or data-center compute, SpaceXAI presents the broadest and most tightly coupled publicly disclosed closure-seeking stack. Its core combines reusable launch, spacecraft manufacturing, orbital communications, terrestrial AI compute and models, an AI1 vehicle design, and a filed orbital-data-center proposal. This is a comparative hypothesis about breadth and coupling, not a claim that competitors do not exist or that a complete self-sustaining stack operates. The actor boundary is load-bearing. The SpaceXAI core is Space Exploration Technologies Corp. and xAI within SpaceX. Tesla remains a separate public company over which SpaceXAI has no control [S95]. Its stationary storage, grid controls, battery-material work, terrestrial manufacturing, chip collaboration, and Optimus program may enter only the explicitly labelled affiliate-hybrid ecosystem. No transfer, availability, orbital qualification, or joint control is presumed. The same discipline applies to every disclosed partner.

The provenance-backed Download original CSV (64 KB) compares that bounded ecosystem with Google/Planet, Starcloud, and Blue Origin. It records the responsible legal entity, relationship, operating environment, maturity, demonstrated capacity, target, missing dependencies, source date, evidence class, common-control status, and off-world reproductive closure. Its Download original CSV (3 KB) puts the bounded SpaceXAI ecosystem first on evidence-weighted breadth: qualifying evidence appears in 17 of 18 layers, with 13 operational, two under development, two stated aspirations, and one no_evidence row. Only 10 of those 17 evidenced layers are under common control. The missing capital-equipment-reproduction layer is itself a minimum cut, and the published filing still records dependence on external materials, components, semiconductors, memory, and compute hardware [S27]. Terafab-specific projects and commitments remain prospective. Consequently, every program has zero demonstrated off-world-closed layers and fails dependency-aware reproductive closure. The 17-layer breadth result is not 94% closure.

The unresolved physical set includes extraterrestrial mining and beneficiation, feedstock-specific refining beyond narrow battery-material routes, qualified bulk metals and polymers, semiconductor fabrication and packaging independent of Earth suppliers, autonomous construction, in-space repair and recycling, and reproduction of machine tools, metrology, optics, bearings, and semiconductor process equipment. Biological life support is outside this article’s uncrewed machine-industry boundary; any settlement or crew-support claim would require a separate closed biological layer rather than inheriting credit from this matrix.

The 18-function evidence crosswalk. Table 23 is an 11-layer descriptive strategy map; it is not a coverage audit. The capacity model has ten coarse sectors. The integrated-bootstrap model resolves the nearest existing minimum-production crosswalk into 18 functions:

  • bulk material: power, mining, refining, and recycling;
  • industrial equipment: robotics, machine tools, construction, thermal, and process equipment/metrology;
  • electronics: interconnects/boards, passives/power, sensors/control, packaging/test, mature logic, and advanced logic/memory;
  • operations and maintenance: transport and repair; and
  • intelligence and compute: compute.

These are model buckets for minimum viable production and service functions, not “the 18 industries that must move off-planet.” Network closure requires enough off-world capacity to reproduce or validly substitute every indispensable node. It does not require relocating every terrestrial firm or all output in an industry.

Nor is 18 an exhaustive count of industrial closure. The same integrated model tracks 17 material categories, while the process-closure gap register still requires species-level chemistry, gases, resists, optics, bearings, calibration artifacts, parent-tool ancestry, qualified source lots, and reproduction of the transport fleet. Thus sector adjacency is a screen over a deeper source–grade–process–tool–fleet graph, not a replacement for it.

The versioned row audit uses Tesla’s current filings and impact disclosures [S90] [S91]. Tesla is a separate public company: shared control, supply agreements, and the Terafab framework make a portfolio crosswalk analytically relevant, but they do not create common ownership or guarantee access to its resources.

SpaceX evidence comes from filing-backed operating and forward-looking disclosures [S27] and the published AI1 specification [S38].

For each sector the audit records the initiative, demonstrated output, location, scale, suppliers, required parent tools, off-world relevance, evidence tier, source locator and date, and residual gap. It then scores seven separate dimensions: capability existence, relevant terrestrial scale, space qualification, off-world operation, local inputs, locally reproducible production equipment, and locally supported repair/verification. These dimensions are never collapsed into one “covered” checkbox.

A sector can be called closed only when source, material-grade, unit-process, critical-part and parent-tool, fleet, failure/substitution, and empirical calibration evidence passes. Portfolio adjacency could reduce coordination or transition cost; it does not prove off-world recipes, yields, autonomous task coverage, commissioning, verification, or economics.

The theoretical advantage is not ownership of complementary companies but a shorter verified end-to-end loop across design → manufacture → deploy → learn. The closure race rewards the shortest such loop, not the largest stock of any single input.

For this portfolio, the proposed sequence is the actor-specific instance of Equation (3): xAI would improve intelligence and automation; factories would expand energy and hardware; Terafab would expand chips; and the resulting terrestrial or orbital compute would feed another verified intelligence-improvement cycle.

The advantage, if it exists, is the ability to integrate feedback, capital allocation, engineering, deployment environments, and industrial production into that shorter loop. Reported preparations for a SpaceX public offering would, if completed, add a financing event for the capital-intensive middle of the loop [S9] [S27]; financing capacity is an enabler, not evidence of closure intent.

III.2 Terafab and the fabrication frontier

What was announced: a Tesla–SpaceX–xAI chip fabrication initiative (March 2026), joined by Intel in April; declared scope from chip design through lithography operation, fabrication, memory, packaging, and test; reported $20B initial plant with a filing-based ceiling near $119B; 2-nm target; mass production stated for 2028 [S6–S10]. What the primary source says [S27]: a general framework with Tesla — timelines, milestones, and capital expenditures for specific projects not yet determined and subject to separate agreements; a stated orbital data-center plan from as early as 2028; and an aim to alleviate potential future chip shortages for orbital AI (Form S-1 pp. 7, 10, 154). First-party messaging versus legal commitment [S29]: the initiative’s own site frames the effort on the Kardashev scale, publishes scaling figures (~1B robots, ~10 Mt/yr launched, >1 TW solar), names chip lines for vehicles, robots, and space (AI5, AI6, D3), publishes an explicit orbital-versus-terrestrial cost decomposition, and names lunar mass drivers as the next step. The divergence between site and filing is itself informative: a strongly space-oriented declared strategy resting on unsettled implementation.

The implementation detail matters. Reporting describes a roughly $3B research fab producing a few thousand wafers per month before any scaled phase, with ambitions moving from about 100,000 wafer starts per month toward one million [S6–S10]. Those figures evidence intended scale, not comparable output: wafer starts cannot be compared with a foundry’s global production without node, wafer diameter, product mix, yield, and effective die output. Planned products include AI5/AI6 chips for vehicles and robots and radiation-tolerant D3 silicon for orbital deployment; Optimus robots have been assigned a stated construction and operating role. Each remains a target rather than demonstrated capacity.

What it changes: fabrication moves from missing term to declared target; the residual dependency moves one layer down (EUV lithography, deposition, etch, metrology, ultra-pure feedstocks — sole-supplier equipment, not foundries); the fab-to-space link becomes explicit (D3). What it does not change: no wafers have been produced; the timeline is faster than any historical ramp; industry skepticism is on record.

The competence question is precise: Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI have no advanced-fab operating record, but Intel plainly does, and the reported process plan is Intel 14A — so the open question is whether that experience transfers into this organizational structure and what obligations Intel has actually accepted, not whether anyone involved has run a fab.

Executed county tax and economic-development agreements strengthen site-level commitment without establishing construction, funding, production, or a definitive operating agreement [S6–S10].6 Wafer-start counts remain incomparable with foundry output without wafer diameter, node, product mix, yield, and effective die output. “One terawatt per year” is a claimed hardware-production rate whose aggregate nameplate power draw would total a terawatt, not a national-electricity-consumption measure.

The lithography question: for terrestrial operation, purchased lithography is an acceptable permanent dependency; for high space closure it must eventually be reproduced, substituted (older nodes at volume; nanoimprint; e-beam), or accepted as designed permanent import — the deepest single closure problem in this framework (and precisely where the Part I strategic-material gap lives). The analysis adds the bottleneck convergence: the AGI-buildout literature identifies advanced packaging and HBM memory as the near-term chip constraints [S35], and HBM is what the Suncatcher radiation testing found most dose-sensitive [S32] — the same component class is the terrestrial scaling bottleneck and the space reliability weak point.

Terafab-specific observables. The milestones that would change this assessment are: the first research-fab wafer and disclosed yield at any node; visible order flow from lithography, deposition, etch, and metrology suppliers; evidence that memory and advanced packaging are actually produced in-house rather than outsourced; radiation-qualified D3 silicon with disclosed orbital-compute unit economics; and definitive agreements that commit capital and counterparties. Industry skepticism is therefore a testable forecast, not a rhetorical counterweight [S10].

  1. The smaller Tesla research fab is at the Giga Texas campus; the proposed scaled SpaceX-led facility is in Grimes County. The distinction matters for interpreting which entity, site, and agreement each source actually covers.↩︎

III.3 Competing hypotheses: the evidence table

The hypotheses are nested rather than exclusive, since a long-run off-world strategy can be pursued through vertical integration and supply hedging — those are mechanisms, not alternatives. H0 is the matched portfolio-adjacency baseline: projects may share ownership, branding, finance, suppliers, data, bilateral interfaces, and ordinary commercial or supply-security motives without sharing one off-world systems architecture. Standalone orbital compute, a domestic fab, launch/AI consolidation, and cross-selling are all H0-compatible. H1 adds deliberate coordinated space–AI–industrial development — the P4a — Documented portfolio direction claim — evidenced most strongly by shared technical interfaces, common architecture documents, binding cross-program milestones, cross-subsidy, or joint resource allocation, not by co-ownership alone. H2 adds an explicit intended transition to recursive industrial closure — the P4b — Recursive-closure intent claim — with closure metrics, a seed bill of materials, minimum-cut work, or locally reproducible production equipment as its distinctive observables. Because the hypotheses nest, each evidence item is assessed on two separate margins — does it separate H1 from H0, and does it separate H2 from H1 — and the assessments are ordinal, not numerical: the items are correlated (several derive from the same corporate communications), absence-items depend on assumed observability, and declared intent is cheap; assigning multiplicable likelihood ratios to such material would imply a probabilistic model that does not exist. Ratings: neutral (equally expected under both), weak, moderate, strong (difficult to explain under the alternative). A distinct motive reading cuts across the nest: heavy industry moves off Earth to protect the biosphere rather than escape a constrained platform [S34] — same physics, different telos — which supplies an additional non-H2 explanation for any orbital-compute observation. Per the propositions ladder, everything here concerns P4, and P3 is decoupled from it: the migration case requires no claim about any company’s intentions.

They are retained as engineering reference-class observations under external cross-checks below — an announced prototype program (satellites slated for early 2027 [S33]), and radiation results bounding the qualification corner (5-yr TID survivability supported with margin; 7-yr system reliability unresolved; II.4).

What the models add to interpretation. A rational H2 actor facing Part I would visibly invest in the electronics closure layer — rad-tolerant lines, stockpile logistics, shelf-life-rated spares, off-world packaging/test — because that is the most frequently observed minimum cut in the sampled ensemble. A rational H1-or-H2 actor facing Part II would run orbital compute at a loss for positioning, or privately believe the COTS/long-life corner; sustained scaled deployment after the unit economics are publicly evident is a moderate-to-strong discriminator between the strategic (H1/H2) and commercial (H0) readings — and conversely, quiet retreat after the demonstration phase is what H0 predicts. On-orbit materials-recovery recycling at scale (not debris-compliance servicing) would be moderate-to-strong for H2 specifically: Part I’s structural result that the LEO architecture lives on its recovered-mass feed loop (capture/mining receives ~98% of central co-binding credit; the analysis withdraws the stronger stale claim that the recycling sector was knockout-indispensable) makes building that loop the rational early move of a LEO-first closure strategy and of no one else.

External cross-checks [S35]: the canonical AGI-buildout analysis resolves the power wall terrestrially without mentioning orbit — non-space-interested corroboration of Part II from outside; its chip bottleneck converges with the space radiation weak point (III.2); and its fast-takeoff thesis, if right, weakens the H1/H2 rationale regardless of the evidence — an effect on the prior, reported separately from the item-level assessments. A provisional July 2026 frontier-lab hiring sweep is quarantined as an appendix note (A.7), not used as an evidence-table item or model input.

Cumulative assessment (ordinal synthesis, not multiplication — the items are correlated and the ratings judgmental): the evidence supports H1 at the level of declared direction but does not establish a coordinated technical architecture. The initiative list in the SEC-filed offering materials (E6) and the first-party messaging (E14) establish an off-world portfolio narrative, while E7/E9/E13 are consistent implementation steps; the matched H0 explains all of them through adjacent commercial, supply-security, financing, and promotional motives unless shared interfaces, milestones, or resource allocation appear. It does not establish H2: no item in Table 25 is more than weakly diagnostic for closure intent, the closure-specific observables (seed bills of materials, reproduction metrics, minimum-cut roadmaps, locally reproducible production equipment) remain absent (E10), and most observed actions are equally expected under a conventional integrated off-world commercial strategy. P4a — Documented portfolio direction is documented; P4b — Recursive-closure intent remains inferential — which is exactly the split encoded by the proposition ladder.

III.4 Control and governance of a self-expanding system

A self-expanding autonomous industrial network is, formally, a governed macroscale von Neumann replicator; the property that makes it valuable — compounding physical replication — makes its failure modes compound too. Verification and authorization must scale with expansion; throttle authority must be explicit (rate limits, hardware-level authorization of replication steps, clarity about who holds them); the legal frame is unsettled and first movers set precedent. Equation (13) therefore counts only capacity admitted by the slowest required reliability, adversarial-verification, secure-command, environmental, treaty, and human-comprehension channel. Reporting gross capacity without this parallel authorized trajectory would hide the governance bottleneck.

The milestone gate in Eq. (45) makes timing non-negotiable: Tctrl≤TAIR&DT_{\mathrm{ctrl}}\le T_{\mathrm{AIR\&D}} and Tctrl≤Tcl,eT_{\mathrm{ctrl}}\le T_{\mathrm{cl},e} for each environment ee whose capacity can replicate. A faster capability or production state is gross capacity, not authorized success, when independent evaluation, command, or stop bandwidth lags it.

The gates depend on consequence, authority, reversibility, containment, and exposure—not on the label “internal” alone. The recursive pipeline has three distinct decisions:

  1. Technical validation: does the proposed change improve the intended held-out capability without unacceptable regression?
  2. Bounded internal authorization: may it advise or act on this monitored, reversible internal task under specified access and rollback limits?
  3. External/public authorization: may it be exposed to broader users, environments, misuse paths, legal duties, and uncontrolled distribution?

Each decision has its own evidence, independence, latency, rollback, and authority requirements. Technical validation is always required before an increment enters the compounding capability account. Internal authorization adds organization-specific controls for privileged data, infrastructure, tools, compute, model-development access, and the consequence of the proposed role. Public authorization adds heterogeneous users and environments, uncontrolled copying, external misuse, product and regulatory obligations, and behavior outside the monitored boundary. Those concerns can overlap without being interchangeable, so one undifferentiated verification yield cannot represent all three gates.

Replication needs a second distinction: productive capacity is not automatically legitimate capacity. The governance sensitivity keeps the accounts separate:

The declared private-race stress case makes the distinction concrete. It reaches 126.222 productive-capacity units after 15 years, so the engineering and owner-objective endpoints pass. Only 2.200 units are legitimately authorized, 124.022 are unauthorized, all 20 contested-resource units are preempted, and the debris-externality stock reaches 85.151. The owner account receives 322.000 cumulative output units while the current-public and future-affected-party accounts receive 28.622 and 7.156. Private net value is positive at 133.300, but social net value is −3,040.566 after the declared externality costs: a negative-sum race and a governance failure despite engineering success. The cooperative and treaty-limited branches both pass the engineering and governance endpoints. These are transparent ASSUMPTION stress tests, not forecasts, legal-title conclusions, or a prescribed distributive ethic.

The claim shares also expose a dynamic institutional risk. Material governance leverage falls from 1.0 to 0.050 in the private-race branch as closure advances. If owner-heavy claims and weak audit or succession rules are fixed during the Earth-dependent bridge, later physical independence can entrench that allocation while removing an effective material control. The control surface must therefore include update authority, resource-claim rules, liability, audit rights, succession of control, and representation of future affected parties—not only stop hardware. Extrasolar abundance and post-ASI allocation remain outside the article’s evidentiary core; they motivate nearer-term institutional design under irreversible scale but do not supply evidence for it. AI 2040 explicitly labels Plan A primarily a recommendation rather than a prediction [S85]; its space supplement motivates the category of claim allocation but supplies no empirical support for the stress-test coefficients. Machine-readable summaries and trajectories are in Download original CSV (3 KB) and Download original CSV (18 KB).

Offline search, simulation, and draft recommendations can use lighter, human-mediated internal gates. Live infrastructure control, destructive experiments, cyber or biological work, physical actuation, model-weight modification, and successor training can require stringent independent controls even when wholly internal. Internal advice is also distinct from internal authority: useful recommendations can arrive while humans retain execution and rollback authority.

Evaluator independence must be demonstrated across model lineage, training data, toolchain, decision authority, and unfiltered audit access. Two monitors that share a strategic blind spot do not supply two independent observations. The matched stress cases in Part I keep the producer trajectory fixed while changing those dependencies; the correlated case fails the authorization endpoint. Human approval likewise becomes ceremonial when proposal throughput exceeds human comprehension throughput. The required response is a throughput interlock, not a larger nominal approval roster.

The framework resolves its own tension — celebrating escape from society-priced costs while requiring retained constraint — through the gateway: in space, permission attaches to launches and spectrum, which is where governance holds enforceable leverage. The leverage variable is dependency — but not proportional to (1 − κ), since this document has already established that scalar closure is invalid and a single low-mass import can be a minimum cut conferring disproportionate leverage. The governing quantity is G_dependency = f(criticality, substitutability, stockpile, supplier concentration, enforceability): what matters is whether withholding an input collapses the network, not how much of it is imported. Part I supplies an answer that is architecture- and parameter-conditioned, and must be stated that way: where import dependency remains load-bearing — the lunar and Mars ensembles — electronics is the most frequently observed minimum cut, and the strategic imported parts are the last material governance handle; in the sampled central LEO draws a single import line is fatal only in a minority of draws (~0–11% for electronics across deterministic regenerations), so there the material handle runs mainly through feed availability and the recovery loop rather than any one import line. Material-dependency governance has a declining window as closure rises; throttle authority, verification requirements, and replication limits are cheapest to embed as licensing conditions during the bridge period. Closure does not end governance (communications, cryptographic authority, personnel, ownership, insurance, treaties, orbital traffic, trade remain), but the material handle is the one that closes.

A serious control architecture — beyond this document’s scope but within its obligation to specify — requires hardware roots of authority; multi-party authorization for replication steps; explicit rate limits; compartmentalization and fault-containment zones; secure update and rollback channels; explicit cyberattack and insider-risk models; independent reliability and adversarial-verification capacity with measured common-mode exposure; an oversight-throughput interlock; operator and government incentive analysis; jurisdiction and liability rules; and failure recovery when communications with Earth are unavailable. These are named requirements, not solved problems. They must be tested under the same loss-of-import, shock, and degraded-communications conditions used to test the production system.

Design principle: replication authority should be the most verified and least autonomous function in the system — positioned deliberately against the efficiency gradient, embedded at the seed stage, because it cannot be retrofitted onto a mature complex.

III.5 Falsifiable indicators, model-ranked

The indicators carry ordinal diagnostic ratings informed by the models (consistent with III.3’s refusal of numerical likelihood ratios; numerical likelihood-ratio language is intentionally excluded):

  1. A terrestrial autonomous-closure demonstrator that constructs and commissions a second production cell under lunar-palette, no-routine-entry constraints — strong for H2 over H1.
  2. Production or fabrication equipment explicitly designed for local extraterrestrial reproduction — strong for H2 over H1.
  3. A dedicated cross-company closure program with published κ-vector metrics — strong for H2 over H1 (flips E10).
  4. A machine-readable off-world seed package containing the physical bill of materials, digital toolchain, industrial memory, dependency graph, and experimental/commissioning plan — strong for H2 over H1.
  5. An element-resolved Moon–Earth–asteroid supply plan with source yields, recovery losses, transfer arcs, import-withdrawal milestones, and explicit strategic-material import stocks — strong for H2 over H1.
  6. Sustained scaled orbital-compute deployment despite publicly evident unfavorable unit economics — moderate-to-strong for H1/H2 over H0 (Part II makes the test operational — watch fleet growth after the economics are public).
  7. Electronics strategic-material-gap engineering: stockpile facilities, shelf-life-rated spares logistics, off-world packaging/test lines — moderate-to-strong for H2 over H1 (Part I makes it the rational first move of a closure strategy).
  8. On-orbit materials-recovery recycling at scale — moderate-to-strong for H2 (the Part I LEO feed-loop result; the indicator rests on feed dependence, not sector indispensability).
  9. An export-control-scoped internal model variant — moderate.
  10. Terafab executed definitive agreements with committed capital — weak-to-moderate (upgrades E7 from framework to program; hedging inside H0 still predicts it).

The ranking above asks which observations discriminate among H0, H1, and H2. A second set asks whether the physical thesis is becoming feasible at all. These lower-diagnosticity but still necessary indicators are retained:

  • robots performing unscripted maintenance, construction, mining, and machine tending for long periods, with autonomous recovery fraction and human intervention hours reported per machine-hour rather than described only as “limited”;
  • task evidence reported with duration, consequence class, verifier class, trial denominator, prompting/checking/recovery/cleanup hours, rollback success, out-of-distribution recovery, and the achieved reliability-ladder rung rather than a benchmark percentage alone;
  • local production of propellant, structural material, and replacement parts at operational rather than laboratory scale;
  • factories using locally processed feedstock to manufacture additional power, extraction, and production equipment;
  • a measured decline in imported mass per unit of local productive capacity, reported by component class rather than as an aggregate mass fraction;
  • element-level closure reported as inputs, inventories, losses, recycled flows, and source-specific yields—not inferred from aggregate local mass;
  • space-manufactured compute, or production equipment capable of making it;
  • net positive industrial reproduction after depreciation — P > D in every indispensable sector — with published r and δ estimates by component class;
  • the Terafab-specific milestones in III.2: first wafer and yield, process equipment orders, in-house memory and packaging, qualified D3 silicon, orbital-compute revenue, and a measured robot reproduction ratio;
  • open-weight systems demonstrating sustained autonomous verified improvement loops — evidence for the threshold-like branch in II.5 — and, separately, fleet- and factory-owning actors outperforming open models on engineering tasks in a way attributable to proprietary process data; the contrary result would show that κ_D does not bind;
  • a sustained measured decline in cost per verified improvement loop, and replication-relevant conditions appearing in launch licenses or export-control terms while material leverage still exists.

The closures also have separate falsifiers; evidence for one must not upgrade the others:
