Glossary

Proposition register

This compact register is validated against the canonical proposition ladder; each descriptive link returns to the definition and current status.

Table G.1. Canonical proposition definitions and current evidential status.
proposition current evidential status
P1 — Conceptual possibility A respectable conceptual case is made; no demonstrated closure is required.
P2 — Technical feasibility Quantitatively explored across named assumption sets; complete-system feasibility is not demonstrated.
P3a — Earth-dependent bridge economics Quantified and negative at anchored values; crossover requires a specific, currently unanchored parameter corner.
P3b — Mature high-closure economics Scenario-modeled but unresolved; neither tested space case becomes self-financing inside 40 years under the declared assumptions.
P4a — Documented portfolio direction The portfolio direction is documented; shared technical interfaces, binding milestones, and joint resource allocation are not publicly established.
P4b — Recursive-closure intent Inferential; no closure program, seed bill of materials, reproduction metric, or minimum-cut roadmap is published.

Technical terms

Recursive self-improvement (RSI): a process in which an intelligent system contributes to producing a more capable successor. This broad category does not itself say that AI R&D is autonomous, verified, or open-ended.

Automated AI R&D: AI execution of some research tasks—such as coding, experiment operation, evaluation, or analysis. Humans may still select problems, supply criteria, authorize deployment, and integrate results, so automation is not verified AI-R&D closure.

Verified AI-R&D closure: a system proposes, implements, tests, independently evaluates, and safely deploys accepted changes to successors within the claimed scope. It does not imply embodied physical autonomy or reproduction of productive capital.

Embodied autonomy: verified ability of an AI-and-hardware system to perform a declared physical task set with bounded intervention, including fault detection and unscripted recovery. It is task- and embodiment-specific; it does not imply AI-R&D closure or capital reproduction.

Reproductive-capital closure: ability of an industrial network to replace and expand every indispensable productive-capital stock after depreciation, obsolescence, and losses. It can exist under a bounded controller and does not imply autonomous AI research.

Authorized replication: productive-capacity growth admitted through the applicable reliability, verification, secure-command, environmental, legal, and human-authority gates. Gross or technically successful replication can remain unauthorized.

Industrial closure (κ): the degree to which a production network internally supplies the critical inputs required for its own operation. The proper object is a sector vector with criticality and substitutability, not a single mass fraction.

Closure engineering: the quantitative discipline, originating in the 1980 NASA/ASEE summer study, of accounting for every input a replicating industrial system must produce or import.

Self-sustaining: able to replace consumed and depreciated productive capacity without an essential external supply.

Self-expanding: able to produce net additional productive capacity after replacement, repair, and losses.

Industrial seed: a compact initial system intended to grow into a broader local production network. In this paper it has four layers: physical equipment; digital models and toolchains; industrial memory; and experimental capacity for generating missing knowledge.

Digital seed: the AI weights, firmware, controllers, compilers, CAD/CAM, simulators, optimization and verification tools, and locally available software dependencies transported with an industrial seed.

Industrial memory: the machine-readable recipes, material and equipment models, calibration and maintenance procedures, build records, failure histories, intervention traces, and provenance required to operate, repair, and adapt the physical seed.

Embodied-autonomy threshold: the task coverage and recovery capability at which a robot-and-AI system can perform the unscripted diagnosis, tool use, construction, repair, learning, and verification needed to keep the industrial graph operating without routine human intervention. It is not a joint-count or robot-count threshold.

Terrestrial autonomous-closure rehearsal: an Earth-based test of the candidate off-world seed under constrained materials, energy, communications, spares, and human access, culminating in construction and commissioning of a second production cell.

Operating-cell equivalent: the integrated layer’s continuous unit of installed, commissioned productive capacity, normalized to the initial seed cell. The reported aggregate-doubling threshold is first passage of this aggregate to 2.0; it is not a claim that a discrete second factory has completed commissioning or that expansion is sustained.

Exogenous deployment: capacity growth supplied by an external industrial base, such as Earth-manufactured data centers delivered to orbit.

Endogenous industrial growth: capacity growth produced from within the industrial network by allocating part of its output to reproducing and expanding productive equipment.

Material vitamins: low-mass, high-criticality inputs—such as advanced chips, dopants, catalysts, specialty chemicals, sensors, bearings, or precision tooling—whose absence can stop a high-mass locally supplied industry.

Process-specific artificial gravity: centrifugal acceleration supplied to a particular machine or production module when microgravity or lunar gravity does not meet that process’s requirements; distinct from rotating an entire habitat or industrial complex.

Clock-setting component: the component with the shortest effective replacement horizon that cannot yet be produced, repaired, substituted, or stockpiled locally; it bounds the survival time of the partially closed system.

Replication time: the time a production network needs to reproduce a unit of productive capacity. It is unknown as a measurement here and appears only as a set-labeled model-output distribution.

Bridge economy: the sequence of independently financeable products and services that carries the system through the capital-intensive stages before closure.

ISRU: in-situ resource utilization — obtaining and using materials at the mission destination rather than importing every supply from Earth.

Productive throughput: the rate at which a system converts energy, materials, compute, and machine time into useful output.

Distributed industrial ecology: a network of specialized, mutually dependent production nodes whose combined input-output graph is self-sustaining or self-expanding.

Scarcity becomes latency: the proposition that, after high closure, the principal limit on many outputs becomes production allocation and completion time rather than external purchase price. Opportunity cost remains.

Von Neumann replicator: a machine system capable of constructing a functional copy of itself from available materials; the formal category to which a fully closed industrial complex belongs.

Terafab: the chip-fabrication initiative announced in March 2026 by Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI and joined by Intel in April, targeting advanced AI chips including radiation-tolerant orbital silicon. The SEC-filed offering materials describe a general framework with unsettled implementation, not a demonstrated fab or legally constituted joint venture [S27].

Society-priced costs: operating inputs priced substantially through human institutions rather than physical conversion alone — land, permitting, interconnection, litigation, and political consent. Space relocates these costs toward gateways such as launch, spectrum, liability, and treaty rather than abolishing them.

Threshold-model argument: the proposition that once a base model crosses the capability needed to run verified improvement loops, a smarter starting model may confer only a transient head start and durable advantage may shift toward hardware doubling time and industrial closure. This is the small-α branch of II.5, not an established law.

Architectural convergence: the point at which the marginal value of another design improvement falls below that of another deployed node. Beyond it, growth is increasingly deployment-limited.

Paradigm-sensitivity split: the division between less paradigm-sensitive layers — energy, labor, transport, and bulk materials — and the more paradigm-specific fabrication layer, where stranding and leapfrog risk concentrate.

Retooling speed: the time a manufacturing complex needs to reconfigure for a new technological paradigm. Alongside hardware doubling time, it is a first-class competitive and resilience metric.

Physical-process data: training-relevant data generated by operating physical industry — telemetry, process settings, intervention records, failures, and fleet or manipulation traces.

Data-advantage index (κ_D): an index over uniqueness, causal linkage, coverage, quality, accessibility, integration, and verification value. Total training-relevant data has no measurable denominator, so κ_D is not a closure ratio.

Unified build record: a per-unit data structure linking design intent (as designed), production parameters (as built), and operational telemetry (as deployed), making physical-process data causally trainable.

Vitamin parts (historical term): the residual imported microelectronics, bearings, precision instruments, catalysts, or other high-complexity inputs that resist local production. The term comes from the 1980 closure literature.

Electronics strategic-material gap: in this model, the unclosable fraction of the electronics sector’s output mix — the results-driving unknown sampled through the space electronics q-scale. It is also called the “vitamin gap” in the closure literature.

Coasean boundary: the organizational boundary at which internal coordination costs equal market transaction costs. AI can lower both sides, so the direction in which the efficient boundary moves is empirical.

Gateway leverage: enforceable governance authority concentrated at dependencies such as launch, spectrum, export control, finance, communications, cryptographic authority, and trade. Its material component follows criticality, substitutability, stockpile, supplier concentration, and enforceability — not the scalar expression (1 − κ).

Minimum cut set: a smallest combination of imported inputs whose loss prevents self-expansion.

Likelihood ratio of evidence: how much more expected an observation is under one hypothesis than under a competitor. Part III uses ordinal diagnosticity rather than numerical multiplication because evidence items are correlated and observability is uncertain.

Maximin growth rate g: the worst-case sector growth rate maximized by the allocation program, ensuring that aggregate growth cannot hide collapse in an indispensable sector.

Assumption set: a named, complete collection of ASSUMPTION-class structural coefficients used together in a model run.

Anchor: a published, source-classed range sampled by Monte Carlo; an anchor constrains an input without converting it into a measurement of the whole system.

Computed: derived mechanically from stated assumptions by the companion model. A computed result inherits the epistemic class of its weakest input.

Kessler syndrome / collisional cascade: an endogenous orbital-debris feedback in which collisions create fragments that increase the probability of later collisions. It is not equivalent to a fixed independent debris hazard.

Sun-synchronous orbit (SSO): a planet-centered precessing orbit selected so that the spacecraft passes a reference point at approximately the same local solar time. Earth SSO is ordinarily a LEO architecture; it does not mean an orbit around the Sun.

Heliocentric orbit: an orbit around the Sun. In the post-lunar scenario, “distributed heliocentric” means separated orbital elements and resource trajectories rather than a new single dense shell.

Sources

Sources [S1–S27] establish the core argument and [S28] identifies the executed companion model. [S29–S36] add corporate, technical, and fast-takeoff/capital-mobilization cross-checks. [S37] is the primary June 2026 Starship V3/V4 disclosure used to normalize the launch-price sensitivity cases; [S38] is the subsequent AI1 product specification. [S39–S44] are the independent spacecraft, thermal, network, microdatacenter, and economic cross-checks for Part II. [S45–S57] bound the lunar, debris, regulatory, and material-source extensions. [S58–S61] ground the digital-loop sensitivity model in scaling and architecture literature; [S62–S66] bound orbital servicing, circularity, mitigation, and collision-control claims; [S67–S68] provide conceptual Earth- and lunar-ascent delta-v anchors without supplying service economics. [S69–S71] define selected authorization, export-control, and debris-plan dependencies; [S72–S75] supply the release-level parameter, token, and five-shot MMLU records used in the chronological backtest. [S76–S78] ground the AI-hardware supply-chain and economic-obsolescence cross-checks. [S79–S85] bound the digital-loop discussion with scenario, company-report, formal-economic, empirical-task, survey, and governance countercases.

Primary statements

[S1] SpaceX, “Mars & Beyond: A City on Mars”.

SpaceX states that establishing a self-sufficient city on Mars requires large-scale cargo and population transfer.

[S2] Tesla, “Master Plan Part 3”.

Tesla outlines a proposed path to a sustainable global energy economy through electrification, renewable generation, and storage.

[S3] xAI, “Company: Accelerating Scientific Discovery”.

xAI describes its mission as accelerating scientific discovery and extending what humanity can know and do.

[S4] NASA, “Overview: In-Situ Resource Utilization”.

NASA describes technologies for using destination resources to produce water, fuel, supplies, and construction capability.

[S5] NASA, “Lunar Surface Technology”.

NASA identifies ISRU, excavation, infrastructure construction, power, robotics, and autonomy as key lunar capabilities.

Reporting and records of the 2026 developments

[S6] Reuters (via Yahoo Finance), March 14, 2026, “Musk says Tesla’s mega AI chip fab project to launch in seven days.”

Confirms the Terafab name, AI5 program, existing TSMC and Samsung partnerships, and earlier remarks about a possible Intel collaboration.

[S7] CBS News, March 23, 2026, “What is Elon Musk’s Terafab chip project?”

Summarizes the Austin announcement and the stated purpose of supplying chips for vehicles, spacecraft, and Optimus robots.

[S8] Proactive Investors (via Yahoo Finance), March 2026, “Musk says Tesla, SpaceX to build $20B Terafab chip plant in Texas.”

Reports the 2-nm target, terrestrial and space chip lines, and the stated 2028 mass-production goal.

[S9] CNBC, May 6, 2026, “Elon Musk’s Terafab chip factory in Texas could cost up to $119 billion, filing shows.”

Reports the filing-based cost ceiling, the roughly $3B research fab, SpaceX’s lead role in the scaled phase, and public-offering preparations.

[S10] Teslarati and Electrek, March 22, 2026, launch coverage and critical commentary.

Together report the proposed venture structure, the SpaceX–xAI merger, D3 orbital chip line, wafer-start ambitions, the Optimus construction role, and skeptical assessments of feasibility. Later primary-source corrections in [S27] control where the reports conflict with the filing.

[S11] SpaceXAI, “Introducing Grok 4.5,” July 2026, with contemporaneous Axios coverage.

Documents an in-house engineering-focused model trained in SpaceXAI data centers, its use in internal engineering work, and reporting on engineering data entering later training runs.

[S12] VentureBeat and Northflank, July 2026, coverage of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 release.

Reports a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model benchmarking near the proprietary frontier on agentic and coding tasks. Used as evidence of benchmark compression, not of an autonomous-R&D threshold.

[S13] Public statements and reporting, July 2026 (Teslarati, Yahoo Tech, and contemporaneous posts on X), on SpaceX engineering data entering a roughly two-trillion-parameter supplemental training run.

Musk states that the engineering corpus, excluding ITAR-restricted material, will enter supplemental training of the next in-house model — the same broad mechanism previously used with acquired coding data.

[S14] Connecting The Dots video commentary, 2026, on Tesla’s internal engineering systems.

Commentary-class source. Its integrated-systems core is corroborated by [S15–S17]; unconfirmed claims of a “Tesla One” brand and a specific manufacturing-CAD AI are excluded from the document’s factual claims.

[S15] Jay Vijayan, on-record interviews and profiles (The Neon Show, Indiaspora, and Forbes India).

Tesla’s first CIO describes building the custom Warp enterprise system in roughly four months in 2012 after rejecting off-the-shelf ERP, and its continuous extension thereafter.

[S16] Stack Overflow engineering blog, “Building the software that helps build SpaceX,” 2021, with corroborating former-engineer accounts.

Documents SpaceX’s internal Warp Drive enterprise and manufacturing systems.

[S17] Tesla AI Day presentations, 2021–2022.

First-party documentation of fleet-learning infrastructure: an occupancy network trained on 1.4 billion fleet frames and auto-labeling replacing roughly five million hours of manual annotation. Later fleet-mile totals are company statements and are not converted into driverless-mile equivalents.

Parameter literature

[S18] D. C. Jordan, S. R. Kurtz, K. VanSant, and J. Newmiller, “Compendium of Photovoltaic Degradation Rates”, Progress in Photovoltaics 24(7), pp. 978–989, 2016.

Meta-study of more than 11,000 measured degradation rates; terrestrial crystalline-silicon median approximately 0.5–0.6% per year.

[S19] W. Q. Lohmeyer, R. J. Aniceto, K. Cahoy, and A. Carlton, “Solar array degradation on geostationary communications satellites: the quantification of annual degradation and degradation over solar proton events”, International Journal of Space Science and Engineering 5(1), pp. 61–81, 2018.

Reported degradation ranges are approximately 0.44–1.03% per year for gallium-arsenide arrays and 0.71–1.69% for silicon arrays. This anchors one component class, not system-wide industrial depreciation.

[S20] S. Philipps and W. Warmuth, Fraunhofer ISE, Photovoltaics Report, July 14, 2026, p. 8; K. P. Bhandari et al., “Energy pay-back time and carbon footprint of commercial photovoltaic systems”, Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews 47, pp. 133–141, 2015.

Energy-payback estimates of roughly 0.9–1.1 years in Europe and a harmonized 1.0–4.1-year range across technologies. These do not measure reproduction of the production system.

[S21] M. Hecht, J. Hoffman et al., MOXIE results, Science Advances, 2022; D. L. Linne, G. B. Sanders, and K. M. Taminger, “Capability and Technology Performance Goals for the Next Step in Affordable Human Exploration of Space”, AIAA 2015-1650, pp. 8–9 and Table VI, also NASA NTRS 20150011681.

Oxygen produced on Mars at gram-per-hour scale at at least 98% purity; lunar oxygen extraction demonstrated at approximately 20% yield and TRL 5/6. Neither is a full-system closure demonstration.

[S22] Independent satellite tracking and reporting by J. McDowell, Harvard-Smithsonian CfA, 2020–2026.

Constellation deorbit and status statistics. Reported fractions near 3% for early generations fall below 0.5% for later ones, and the tracker separates early deorbit, uncontrolled decay, retirement, and disposal. Without cohort, observation interval, and satellite-years, these are fleet fractions rather than hazard rates.

Closure-engineering literature

[S23] NASA, Advanced Automation for Space Missions (NASA CP-2255), 1980 NASA/ASEE summer study; matter-closure and residual-import statements at sec. 5.3.6, report p. 219 (PDF p. 225).

Designs a proof-of-principle self-replicating lunar factory from a roughly 100-ton seed. It adopts a one-year strawman replication target whose component values it calls crude estimates; cites 90–96% closure from earlier studies of specific nonreplicating production applications; and places rigorous demonstration of complete parts closure outside its scope. These are design assumptions and plausibility arguments, not demonstrated performance.

[S24] R. A. Freitas Jr. and R. C. Merkle, Kinematic Self-Replicating Machines, Landes Bioscience, 2004.

Comprehensive survey of the design space for physical self-replicating systems.

Economics and progress-rate literature

[S25] R. H. Coase, “The Nature of the Firm,” Economica 4(16), 1937.

Transaction-cost account of firm boundaries used in II.5’s integration-versus-modularity analysis.

[S26] Epoch AI (Ho et al.), “Algorithmic Progress in Language Models,” 2024.

Estimates that compute required for fixed language-model performance halves roughly every eight months. The resulting approximately threefold-per-year rate does not license extrapolation to autonomous research or physical productivity.

Primary regulatory filing and model provenance

[S27] Space Exploration Technologies Corp., Form S-1 registration statement, filed May 20, 2026, SEC accession 0001628280-26-036936; and Rule 433 free-writing prospectus, filed June 4, 2026, SEC accession 0001628280-26-040610, with associated June 4 offering materials; contemporaneous analysis by Electrek, Tom’s Hardware, Forbes, and KBTX.

This document’s primary corporate source. On Terafab it describes a general framework with Tesla; specific projects, timelines, milestones, and capital expenditures require separate agreements and were not yet determined (Form S-1 pp. 7, 10, 154). Risk Factors characterize the orbital-AI, lunar, and interplanetary initiatives as early-stage, unproven, and potentially unsuccessful (pp. 12, 24–25). The initiative list includes terrestrial and orbital AI compute, orbital data centers from as early as 2028, internal chip design and manufacture, lunar manufacturing and energy, in-orbit manufacturing, manufacturing on the Moon and Mars, asteroid mining, and “interplanetary industrialization” (pp. 164, 171; Rule 433 roadshow slides 42–44). It reports more than 1,000 automated collision-avoidance maneuvers per day across Starlink in 2025 (pp. 9, 153). These and the other load-bearing [S27] extractions are recorded in params/claim_provenance.yaml and the generated Download original CSV (40 KB).

[S28] Companion simulation program, rsi-model repository, r4.0 release candidate on branch main; concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21619447; Appendices C–D.

Reproducibility source, not evidence. It computes consequences of stated assumptions and supports no empirical claim on its own authority. Each archived release tag mints a version-specific DOI.

Corporate and orbital-compute record

[S29] Terafab official project site (terafab.ai), accessed July 2026.

First-party messaging: combined logic, memory, and advanced packaging; Kardashev-scale framing; scaling figures of approximately one billion robots, ten million tonnes per year launched to orbit, and more than one terawatt of solar; AI5/AI6/D3 lines; an explicit Earth-versus-space cost decomposition; and lunar mass drivers as a next step. Marketing and recruiting material — evidence of declared intent, not commitment.

[S30] Waymo safety-impact disclosures, 2026.

Cumulative fully driverless miles used as the comparison point in I.2 and Appendix A.3. No conversion to supervised autonomy miles is made.

[S31] Heavy-lift flight-test reporting, 2026.

Cumulative count of thirteen test flights through mid-2026, used as a low-volume, high-information development proxy rather than a capacity or reliability input.

[S32] B. Agüera y Arcas, T. Beals, M. Biggs, J. V. Bloom, T. Fischbacher, K. Gromov, U. Köster, R. Pravahan, and J. Manyika (Google), “Towards a future space-based, highly scalable AI infrastructure system design,” arXiv:2511.19468 (v1 November 22, 2025; v2 June 17, 2026, the version carrying the detailed figures cited here), with the Project Suncatcher blog post.

Technical design study for satellite accelerator clusters: 67 MeV proton-beam testing of a Trillium TPU v6e, with HBM most TID-sensitive (irregularities from 2 krad(Si) against a 750 rad(Si) five-year requirement, no hard TID failures to 15 krad(Si)) and core logic/on-chip SRAM most SEE-sensitive; an inference error estimate near one per 3×10⁶ inferences under stated assumptions, with training impact reserved; an 81-satellite, 1 km-radius cluster near 650 km in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit; and 800 Gbps unidirectional optical links against a roughly 10 Tbps per-link requirement. The authors twice state that the cost section is not a full economic analysis: it compares amortized launch cost per kW-year ($810 for a Starlink-v2-class ratio and $810–7,500 across classes at $200/kg) with terrestrial electricity spend ($570–3,000/kW-year), excluding buildings, infrastructure, and chips. Reaching approximately $200/kg by 2035 requires about 370,000 tonnes of additional cumulative launch mass, or roughly 1,800 Starship-class flights averaging 180 per year. Thermal management, ground communications, reliability, and repair remain open; orbital repair is described as impracticable and redundant provisioning proposed instead.

[S33] SpaceNews, Via Satellite, and Data Center Dynamics coverage of orbital-compute programs, 2025–2026.

Reports the Google–Planet partnership, two prototype satellites slated for launch by early 2027, the research-stage status of the program, and at least one additional entrant flying an accelerator demonstrator.

[S34] Will Marshall, co-founder and CEO of Planet Labs, interviewed on the Moonshots podcast with P. Diamandis and colleagues, episode 266, published June 26, 2026. A transcript with paragraph timestamps is archived at docs/transcripts/moonshots-266-2026-06-26.md.

Cited for mechanisms rather than measurements: launch tax versus compute tax (0:00:22 and 1:17:49); matching low-orbit decay life to hardware obsolescence; payload cost-performance outpacing launch cost-performance; limits on reproducing historical archives; finite compute-demand possibility; the protect-the-biosphere telos; and the recollected Google/Planet $200–300/kg crossover study (0:52:07). Recollections and projections are unverified.

External strategic cross-check

[S35] L. Aschenbrenner, Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead, June 2024, archived in docs/sources/.

Analyst estimates used as external cross-checks: a trillion-dollar compute-cluster trajectory; power as the binding constraint with a politically conditional natural-gas floor; CoWoS/HBM as chip bottlenecks; a fast-takeoff thesis; and historical capital-mobilization reference classes. These claims affect priors and counterfactuals, not the evidence table’s item-level assessment.

Contextual engineering and reporting sources

[S36] Assorted company disclosures, industry reporting, agency guidance, price sheets, and technical literature used to bound Appendix A and Part II scenarios.

Covers evidence not carried by [S18–S23]: foundry equipment-depreciation schedules (2–5 years); data-center accelerator retirement practice (3–6 years); a large-training-run disclosure of roughly 419 interruptions over 54 days across approximately 16,000 accelerators (cluster interruption frequency, not component hazard); 2019 reporting on factory construction cadence; 2026 humanoid-robot production targets; NASA small-spacecraft guidance on altitude-, ballistic-coefficient-, and solar-activity-dependent decay; launch price sheets; flexible-array and deployable-radiator performance; accelerator system pricing; AI-optimized data-center capex and PUE; and nuclear-restart PPA reporting. No single permanent identifier covers the collection. The r4.0 claim-level audit therefore does not use [S36] to justify any non-ASSUMPTION model endpoint. Ranges synthesized from these materials remain explicitly ASSUMPTION; [S36] supplies contextual bounds only. Every retained non-assumption endpoint instead has an exact record in params/claim_provenance.yaml.

[S37] Space Exploration Technologies Corp., European Union Prospectus, approved by BaFin, June 5, 2026, pp. 63, 70–72, 80–82, 97, and 137; see also the June 4, 2026 SEC-filed roadshow materials.

Primary company disclosure for the Starship aspiration normalization. It states that fully reusable Starship V3 is expected to carry 100 metric tonnes to orbit, that future generations could reach 200 tonnes potentially as soon as V4, and that Starship is intended eventually to reduce a cited historical $18,500/kg launch-cost benchmark by 99% or more. The resulting ≤$185/kg figure is arithmetic, not a quoted V3/V4 customer price. The $100/kg and $30–50/kg cases in Part II are progressively more aggressive sensitivity axes and are not attributed to this source. The prospectus also uses 100 kW/t to describe a long-term path to 100 GW of orbital AI-compute power per year—about one million tonnes and thousands of launches annually—and identifies full rapid reuse, approvals, spectrum, and long-duration reliability as dependencies. It warns that terrestrial energy improvements could diminish orbital viability. The target extraction and arithmetic are archived in docs/sources/spacex-ai-aspirations-2026-06.md.

[S38] Space Exploration Technologies Corp., Starmind AI1 official product page, accessed July 27, 2026; numeric provenance snapshot archived at docs/sources/starmind-ai1-2026-07-27.md.

First-party architecture disclosure for a planned orbital AI satellite: 150 kW peak / 120 kW average compute payload, 70 kW/tonne vehicle efficiency, 150 kW solar array at 250 W/m², 110 m² deployable liquid radiator, and a 20 m by 70 m deployed envelope. It also describes redundant pumped loops, debris shielding, laser links through Starlink, and sun-synchronous operation, but does not disclose vehicle capex, component mass, achieved availability, service life, qualification cost, or link cost. Company specification, not demonstrated performance.

Post-IPO orbital-compute calibration

[S39] S. G. Turyshev, “Orbital Data Centers: Spacecraft Constraints and Economic Viability”, arXiv:2604.27197, submitted April 29, 2026. The values used across [S39–S44] are consolidated in docs/sources/orbital-compute-calibration-2026-07-27.md.

Independent system-level closure across power, eclipse storage, thermal rejection, spacecraft fixed mass, communication intensity, utilization, finite life, and economics. Its representative 1 MW high-sunlight case requires 5,640 m² of BOL PV, 2,500 m² of radiator, 29.4 kg/kW for PV, storage, and radiators, and 34–59 kg/kW total after fixed spacecraft functions. At 40 kg/kW, $10,000–40,000/kW of terrestrial infrastructure permits only $250–1,000/kg for launch and spacecraft build combined before communications, operations, utilization, and life penalties. The paper’s annual-hazard penalties are illustrative sensitivities, not fleet measurements.

[S40] S. Gaalema, S. Indyk, and C. Staley, “Reduced-Mass Orbital AI Inference via Integrated Solar, Compute, and Radiator Panels”, arXiv:2604.07760, April 2026; and I. Bargatin, D. Jin, Z. Alansari, and J. R. Raney, “Tether-Based Architecture for Solar-Powered Orbital AI Data Centers”, arXiv:2512.09044 and AIAA SciTech 2026.

Low-mass inference architecture studies. The first reports a design basis above 100 kW/t using integrated PV, vapor-chamber radiators, and custom accelerators in a kilometer-scale array; its large example is about 150 tonnes and 16 MW. The second proposes 2–20 MW tethered systems with approximately 10 kg, 2 kW nodes. Both make mass-reducing integration assumptions whose deployment, dynamics, thermal, shielding, qualification, and lifetime closure remains prospective.

[S41] K. van Berkel, “The Cost and Network Limits of Space-Based AI Compute”, arXiv:2607.14172, submitted July 15, 2026.

Post-IPO compute-network comparison. For the modeled 8,000-accelerator systems, the terrestrial Clos fabric has 28,800 TB/s bisection bandwidth versus 2.25 TB/s for a two-dimensional and 10 TB/s for a three-dimensional orbital mesh at 100 Gbps links; estimated network latency is 150–450 times higher. The paper finds orbital inference potentially feasible but frontier LLM training uncompetitive on the analyzed meshes. Its aggressive $/kg and kg/kW economic premises are used here only as context; the network calculation is the calibration result.

[S42] R. Eason, N. Bleier, M. Lembeck, and R. Kumar, “Architecting Space Microdatacenters: A System-level Approach”, IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture, 2025.

Peer-reviewed cost/performance study of bespoke 0.5–10 kW microdatacenters for space-native workloads. Power and thermal functions account for roughly a third of modeled spacecraft TCO, compute hardware can be less than one percent, and energy-efficiency improvements are up to 2.5 times more valuable in space and reduce modeled TCO by approximately two-thirds. Its scale and in-orbit data origin differ from the Part II terrestrial-substitution case.

[S43] NASA Glenn Research Center, NASA/TM—2005-213442, radiator mass comparison, 2005.

Primary engineering reference separating radiator panels from the complete heat-transport and deployment system. ISS two-sided panels are reported at 2.75 kg/m² and 8.8 kg/m² after fluid loop and deployment mechanism; the JIMO analysis estimated 5 kg/m² for the complete system. At 353 K, 0.86 emissivity, and 173 K environment, the sizing example uses approximately 1.4 m²/kW. These are heritage/system cross-checks, not forecasts for an optimized AI1 radiator.

[S44] University of Virginia National Security Data Policy Institute, “Evaluating Space-Based Data Center Architectures: Capabilities, Constraints, and Trade-Offs”, Product No. 00036, May 19, 2026.

Policy synthesis with a simplified public cost model. Its representative five-year 1 GW estimates are $135.6 billion orbital versus $16.6 billion terrestrial under present-style assumptions, and $15.4 billion orbital only when launch falls to $30/kg, satellite hardware to $10/W, specific power rises to 100 W/kg, sunlight availability to 80%, and annual degradation and GPU failures each fall to 1%. It excludes GPU hardware, financing, insurance, logistics overhead, and downtime, so it is used only as a directional joint-condition check.

Lunar surface–orbit architecture and debris boundary

[S45] D. J. Kessler and B. G. Cour-Palais, “Collision Frequency of Artificial Satellites: The Creation of a Debris Belt”, Journal of Geophysical Research 83(A6), 2637–2646, 1978.

The original collision-feedback result: satellite collisions create orbiting fragments, each of which raises the probability of later collisions. It supplies the direction of the feedback, not a universal threshold for a particular future constellation.

[S46] N. R. Boone and R. A. Bettinger, “Simulation of Debris Events in Selected Low Lunar Orbits”, Journal of the Astronautical Sciences 70, 16 (2023).

Approximately 97,000 simulated fragments across eight breakup cases show orbit-dependent debris evolution: some selected low lunar orbits retain long-lasting populations, while impacts on the Moon are geographically nonuniform. The reported one-year collision probabilities are low for the notional present cases; the paper does not establish a current lunar cascade.

[S47] NASA, “Artemis Base Camp on the Moon Will Need Light, Water, Elevation”, 2021; NASA, “Lunar Dust Mitigation: A Guide and Reference”, 2021; and NASA, “Archway for Radiation and Micrometeorite Occurrence Resistance”, 2013.

Surface-architecture boundary references: south-polar illumination and access to shadowed volatile deposits; abrasive/electrostatic dust effects on radiators, mechanisms, and sensors; and local regolith as candidate bulk radiation and micrometeoroid shielding. None establishes reserve economics, continuous power at a selected site, or industrial closure.

[S48] D. C. Davis, F. S. Khoury, K. C. Howell, and D. J. Sweeney, “Phase Control and Eclipse Avoidance in Near Rectilinear Halo Orbits”, AAS Guidance, Navigation and Control Conference, 2020.

The Gateway reference NRHO is designed around eclipse avoidance, resonance, and low-cost stationkeeping with active phase control. It supports the gateway/service-layer role but does not make NRHO a passive, resource-bearing industrial site.

[S49] NASA, “Basics of Space Flight: Planetary Orbits”, updated 2024.

Defines a Sun-synchronous orbit as a planet-centered precessing orbit that preserves local solar time and distinguishes it from a heliocentric orbit around the Sun.

Orbital-data-center regulatory record

[S50] Federal Communications Commission, Space Bureau, “Space Bureau Accepts for Filing SpaceX’s Application for Orbital Data Centers”, Public Notice DA 26-113, released February 4, 2026; ICFS File No. SAT-LOA-20260108-00016, Call Sign S00798, application filed January 30, 2026.

The notice accepts for filing an application describing a non-geostationary system of up to one million satellites. Acceptance for filing begins public and regulatory review; it is not authorization to deploy or operate the proposed system.

Integrated bootstrap and material-source record

[S51] NASA Science, “Moon Composition & Structure”, updated July 23, 2026.

NASA lists oxygen, silicon, magnesium, iron, calcium, and aluminum as the principal elements in lunar-crust minerals, with smaller titanium, uranium, thorium, potassium, and hydrogen, and distinguishes calcium/aluminum-rich highlands from iron/titanium-rich maria. This is a bulk-composition boundary, not a resource or reserve estimate.

[S52] Jennifer Edmonson and Doug Rickman, “A Survey of Geologic Resources”, NASA Technical Reports Server record 20120015479, 2012.

The lunar-geology survey gives an average regolith bulk density of about 1.5 g/cm³ (1.5 t/m³), used only for the illustrative in-place inventory calculation in I.9. Density does not determine grade, recovery, or reserve economics.

[S53] P. G. Lucey, G. J. Taylor, and E. Malaret, “Abundance and Distribution of Iron on the Moon”, Science 268(5214), 1150–1153, 1995.

Near-global Clementine data produced an approximately 3 wt% iron estimate for the lunar highlands crust and approximately 7–8 wt% for lower-crustal material exposed by South Pole–Aitken. The 3% value is used as a conservative illustrative concentration, not a claim about a selected mining site.

[S54] C. B. Moore, C. F. Lewis, E. K. Gibson, and W. Nichiporuk, “Total Carbon and Nitrogen Abundances in Lunar Samples”, Science 167(3918), 495–497, 1970.

Returned bulk fines in the reported samples contained carbon and nitrogen at roughly hundreds of parts per million, with mixtures of indigenous, meteoritic, and solar-wind contributions. The result establishes scarcity in those samples, not a global lunar resource map.

[S55] NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, “NASA’s LRO: Lunar Ice Deposits Are Widespread”, October 3, 2024.

LRO analysis finds widespread evidence of water ice in permanently shadowed regions beyond the immediate south pole while explicitly stating that deposit volume and burial beneath dry regolith cannot yet be accurately determined. Occurrence is not a bankable reserve.

[S56] NASA Science, “OSIRIS-REx Frequently Asked Questions”, accessed July 27, 2026.

Laboratory analysis of returned Bennu material reports abundant organic molecules and sodium-rich minerals associated with evaporation of water. One carbonaceous sample demonstrates possible volatile and carbon-bearing diversity; it does not establish asteroid-mining yield or economics.

[S57] NASA, “Lunar Surface Technology”, accessed July 27, 2026.

NASA describes Blue Alchemist’s integrated autonomous processing of regolith simulant into silicon solar cells, aluminum wires, oxygen, iron, and slag; it also reports vacuum extraction of oxygen from simulant by a molten-regolith-electrolysis reactor. These are subsystem and prototype demonstrations, not autonomous lunar industrial closure.

Digital scaling and architecture record

[S58] J. Kaplan et al., “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models”, arXiv:2001.08361, 2020.

Reports empirical power-law relationships between cross-entropy loss and model size, dataset size, and training compute over the studied ranges. These are loss curves for specified model families and data regimes, not a law of scalar intelligence or recursive improvement.

[S59] J. Hoffmann et al., “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models”, arXiv:2203.15556, 2022.

Trains more than 400 models and finds that, in the studied Transformer regime, compute-optimal model size and training-token count should increase together. Chinchilla outperforms larger undertrained models at the same training-compute budget. The result constrains resource allocation; it does not demonstrate RSI.

[S60] A. Gu and T. Dao, “Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces”, arXiv:2312.00752, 2023.

Introduces a selective state-space architecture with hardware-aware recurrent computation, linear sequence-length scaling, and reported throughput and quality comparisons to same-size Transformers. The results establish an architecture-specific trade space, not universal superiority across training, inference, hardware, and task regimes.

[S61] W. Fedus, B. Zoph, and N. Shazeer, “Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity”, arXiv:2101.03961, 2021.

Demonstrates sparsely activated mixture-of-experts training while documenting routing, communication, precision, load-balancing, and instability challenges. Total parameters and active parameters per token are therefore different resource quantities.

Separates robotic manipulation, rendezvous and capture, relocation, planned and unplanned repair, refueling, manufacturing, inspection, and recycling, reuse, and repurposing into distinct capability areas. It records both operational precedents and developmental systems; inclusion is not evidence of fleet-scale economic closure.

[S63] NASA, “On-orbit Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing 1 (OSAM-1)”, status updated March 23, 2026.

NASA records the decision to cancel OSAM-1 after independent review found major technical, integration, schedule, cost, mission-risk, return, and transition-partner problems. The case is direct counterevidence to assuming that autonomous servicing of an unprepared spacecraft is already routine or economical.

ESA describes rendezvous and capture of an unprepared, uncooperative object as precise and complex, notes that removal is costly and not always possible, and treats ClearSpace-1 as a future demonstration rather than an operational recycling service.

[S65] NASA Orbital Debris Program Office, “Debris Mitigation”; F. J. Krage, NASA Spacecraft Conjunction Assessment and Collision Avoidance Best Practices Handbook, Revision 1, NASA/SP-20230002470, 2023.

NASA separates prevention of debris creation, design against small impacts, selection of lower-risk regimes, post-mission disposal, trackability, conjunction screening, risk assessment, maneuverability, reliability, and operator coordination. These practices define control functions but do not calibrate a future large orbital industrial network.

[S66] European Space Agency, Space Environment Report 2025, April 1, 2025.

Reports that mitigation compliance is improving but remains insufficient, that fragmentation adds objects faster than natural clearance in important regimes, and that debris can continue growing without new launches. ESA presents active removal as necessary to arrest that feedback; the report does not specify one universal constellation threshold.

[S67] A. Beaurain, A. Souchier, M. Moravie, R. L. Sackheim, and H. A. Cikanek III, “Earth-to-Orbit Rocket Propulsion”, NASA Technical Reports Server record 20030066115, March 31, 2003.

The abstract identifies approximately 9 km/s as the effective requirement to reach Earth parking orbit after gravity and atmospheric-drag effects. It is retained as a historical conceptual-design anchor, not a current launch vehicle performance or cost estimate.

[S68] T. A. Lewis, E. L. Judd, Z. D. May, and R. T. Joyce, “A Parametric Assessment of Lunar and Mars Ascent Vehicle Synergy”, AIAA ASCEND 2020, NASA Technical Reports Server record 20205007701, 2020, p. 4, Table 2 and Section III.A.

Table 2 reports 1,850 m/s from the lunar surface to low lunar orbit and the text rounds the one-way ascent cases to 1.9 km/s for LLO and 2.7 km/s for NRHO. The paper derives vehicle mass with the rocket equation and notes that route values depend on vehicle thrust-to-weight and specific impulse. These values do not establish dollars per kilogram or the economics of a lunar service network.

These provisions make consent, authorization, liability, and custody explicit decision gates; this manuscript does not offer a legal conclusion for any specific mission.

The current rule treats certain transfers of registration, control, or ownership of spacecraft—including spacecraft providing logistics, assembly, or servicing—as exports. The peer-reviewed two-asset model treats specialized AI hardware as economically obsolete much faster than conventional capital and reports an approximately seven-quarter AI-capacity adjustment half-life in its advanced-economy calibration. It is used as a conceptual cross-check for separating physical survival from economic replacement; its terrestrial macro calibration is not transferred into the off-world cohort sensitivity.

The essay explicitly presents educated guesses rather than established forecasts. Its “country of geniuses in a datacenter” assumes millions of digital workers operating 10–100 times faster than humans, then organizes their limits around the marginal returns to intelligence: outside-world speed, data, intrinsic complexity, human constraints, and physical law. The article itself warns that lines of code overstate productivity and that the poll’s true uplift was probably lower. It also reports strong execution against fixed experimental goals while identifying goal selection, research taste, and autonomous successor design as remaining gaps. All figures are company_statement, subject to selection, attribution, evaluator, and counterfactual bias; none becomes a capability-growth coefficient.

Its growth results depend on substitution, saving and depreciation, research returns to scale and parallelizability, and fixed natural-resource factors; R&D automation alone need not create explosive growth. This is the closest formal economic lineage for the manuscript’s two closures. Its capital is aggregate, whereas this article requires every indispensable sector to replace and expand; it does not prove that an off-world engineering graph closes. Its limitations note says the metric is serial human labor replaced at 50% success, not uninterrupted autonomous work; varies by orders of magnitude across domains; is not a delegation threshold; and does not directly determine automation or research speedup. The filing and program page describe Tesla’s separate energy, manufacturing, AI, battery-material, semiconductor, and Optimus programs. They establish related-party transactions and portfolio adjacency, not SpaceXAI ownership, guaranteed transfer, orbital qualification, availability, or joint control.

[S96] OpenAI, “Our updated Preparedness Framework”, April 15, 2025; and Preparedness Framework, version 2, April 15, 2025, AI Self-Improvement capability thresholds; accessed July 29, 2026.

Version 2 makes AI Self-Improvement a tracked category. Its High threshold is comparable to giving every OpenAI researcher a strong mid-career research-engineer assistant relative to a 2024 baseline. Its Critical threshold includes a superhuman research-scientist agent or sustained generational model improvement in roughly one-fifth of 2024-equivalent wall-clock time. These are company-defined governance thresholds, not evidence that either has been reached.

[S97] Giulio Starace et al., “PaperBench: Evaluating AI’s Ability to Replicate AI Research”, initial release, April 2, 2025; accompanying paper and open-source scaffold; accessed July 29, 2026.

PaperBench asks agents to reproduce 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight or Oral papers from scratch and grades 8,316 author-developed rubric items. The best initial tested configuration—Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) with the open-source scaffold—averaged 21.0% and did not outperform the reported top-ML-PhD subset baseline. It measures research replication and engineering, not autonomous research direction or recurring successor-model improvement.

[S98] OpenAI, GPT-5.6 System Card, published July 9, 2026, secs. 1 and 9.1.3; accessed July 29, 2026.

OpenAI assessed GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna below its High AI Self-Improvement threshold as of publication. The evaluation suite includes Internal Research Debugging, KernelGen 1P, NanoGPT, PostTrainBench Lite, MLE-Bench Revised and externally run METR Time Horizon 1.1. The card records task, budget, gaming, contamination, scaffold and scale qualifications; METR did not regard the GPT-5.6 time-horizon estimate as robust because of unusually high detected cheating. “Below High” does not imply no useful acceleration, no risk or general safety.

[S99] OpenAI, “Strengthening our safety ecosystem with external testing”, November 19, 2025; accessed July 29, 2026.

OpenAI distinguishes independently run evaluations, methodology review and subject-matter-expert probing. It also describes access, confidentiality, publication review and compensation boundaries. An external evaluator adds independence but does not make a non-public task fully reproducible; the model snapshot, harness, budget and publication constraints remain part of the evidence.

[S100] Google DeepMind, An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security, April 2025, executive summary and secs. 2.3 and 3.4; and “Taking a responsible path to AGI”, April 2, 2025; accessed July 29, 2026.

The paper treats automated scientific R&D as a possible positive feedback: better AI systems enable more automated R&D, which can produce still better systems. It expects near-term recursive improvement to resemble AI systems doing human-like AI research rather than directly editing their own weights. Its paradigm-continuation, uncertain-timeline, accelerating-growth and approximate-continuity premises are explicit assumptions, not measured forecasts, and the paper does not claim to cover every superintelligence risk.

[S101] Google DeepMind, Frontier Safety Framework, version 3.1, published April 17, 2026, secs. 3.1–3.2; and “Google DeepMind strengthens the Frontier Safety Framework”, April 17, 2026; accessed July 29, 2026.

Version 3.1 defines ML R&D acceleration level 1 as realized AI progress substantially beyond historical rates and ML R&D automation level 1 as the ability to automate any Google AI-capabilities research team’s work at approximately comparable all-inclusive cost. It expects acceleration from systems of models integrated with workflows rather than a model alone and distinguishes external deployment from high-risk internal deployment. Neither threshold is identical to verified, safely deployed, recurring successor-model closure.

[S102] Space Exploration Technologies Corp., response to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, comment 7, May 7, 2026, pp. 5–6 and 24–25; accessed July 29, 2026.

SpaceX defines cost per token as a function of model, compute hardware, and energy; identifies compute depreciation as the largest current component; and describes proprietary chips and orbital solar as intended hardware- and energy-cost advantages. It also states that no specific comparable cost-per-token figure is disclosed, that the metric was not then used for performance evaluation or resource allocation, and that it remains evolving. The response separately confirms that capitalized internal satellite launch cost includes allocated launch-vehicle depreciation.

[S103] World Economic Forum, “Conversation with Elon Musk”, January 22, 2026, 16:30–17:00 CET; official transcript; accessed July 29, 2026.

Musk predicted that space would become the lowest-cost place to put AI within two years, or three at the latest. This article fixes the resulting comparison window at January 22, 2028 through January 22, 2029 and preserves the ambiguity of “place to put AI.” The personal statement is a falsifiable comparison target, not engineering evidence or a model prior.
